questions.pre_read: Note exactly when the scanners fail, and what else is happening at that moment.
questions.correct_explanation: Microwave ovens give off energy in the 2.4 GHz band that many Wi-Fi networks use, so the scanners' radio signal is drowned out. That is a physical-layer problem, so the fix is physical too: a band or channel the oven does not reach. Raising transmit power is the runner-up because a stronger signal can push through some noise, but the scanners would still share the oven's band.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because dropped connections can come from address problems. But the drops follow the oven, not address changes; fixed addresses cannot clear radio noise.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a stronger signal can outshout some noise. But the oven floods the same band, so drops continue; changing band avoids the clash.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a VLAN gives the scanners their own logical network. But it separates frames at layer 2; the radio noise sits below that.

tips: Eliminate: A changes addressing at layer 3, and D separates frames at layer 2; neither touches the radio noise the oven makes.
Final two: B beats C because the oven floods the same band; more power still shares the noise, while another band avoids it.
Exam cue: name the layer before choosing the fix. A control helps only at the layer where the problem lives.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-153 Section 3.1.1 (Attack Monitoring: interference from other devices can deny WLAN service); NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1 Section 2.1 (The Need for Network Layer Security: controls at each layer)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a control protects only its own layer; name the layer before the fix' (notes 4.1.2 The OSI Model (+4.1.10 Wireless Security: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Blind re-test fix (30 Oct 2026): runner-up is now a radio-layer lure (more power). Cross-review fix (31 Oct 2026): provenance now also cites notes 4.1.10, which carries the 2.4 GHz interference fact.

questions.question: A public library's print server has FTP, Telnet, HTTPS and the printing port open, but staff use only printing and the HTTPS admin page. Which change should the system administrator propose as BEST?

options.A: Have the IDS alert whenever FTP or Telnet is used
options.B: Replace FTP and Telnet with SFTP and SSH on the server
options.C: Encrypt the server's disk to protect stored print jobs
options.D: Turn off the FTP and Telnet services on the server

questions.key_concept: Every open port is a way in; services nobody needs should be turned off, not just made more secure.
questions.pre_read: Compare what each option changes on the server, and what it leaves exposed afterward.
questions.correct_explanation: No one uses FTP or Telnet on this server, so the safest change is to turn them off: a service that is not running cannot be attacked. Replacing them with SFTP and SSH is the runner-up because it encrypts the logins, but it keeps two services running that nobody needs, each still a way in.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because alerts reveal misuse. But detection only reports use after it happens; turning off the unused services removes the risk entirely.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: SFTP and SSH are the encrypted versions of these services. But no one needs them here; unneeded services, even encrypted ones, still leave extra ways in.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption protects data. But disk encryption guards stored files, not the open network services an attacker could log in through.

tips: Eliminate: A only detects use of services that need not run, and C protects stored data, not open network services.
Final two: D beats B because services nobody needs should not run at all; encrypting them still leaves extra ways in.
Exam cue: first ask whether a service is needed. If not, turn it off; secure only what must stay.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-7 (Least Functionality)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'expose only the services the business needs' (notes 4.1.5 Ports, Protocols and Secure Alternatives). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. Host and network sensors
questions.question: A credit union wants to spot suspicious activity on its loan server, but almost all traffic to the server is encrypted. Which detection control should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: A network IDS sensor on the loan server's own segment
options.B: An inline IPS at the credit union's internet edge
options.C: A host-based IDS agent installed on the loan server
options.D: A weekly review of the edge firewall's logs

questions.key_concept: Network sensors cannot read encrypted traffic; a host-based IDS on the server sees activity after decryption.
questions.pre_read: Consider where each control sits and what it can actually observe from there.
questions.correct_explanation: Network sensors see packets on the wire, and here nearly all of them are encrypted, so they cannot read the activity inside. A host-based IDS agent runs on the loan server itself, where traffic is already decrypted, and watches its logs, files and processes. A network IDS on the segment is the runner-up: well placed, but blind to the encrypted content.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it watches the right segment. But a network sensor reads packets on the wire, and encryption hides what is happening inside the sessions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because an inline IPS can block attacks. But at the internet edge it misses internal traffic and still cannot read the encrypted sessions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because firewall logs record connections. But a weekly review is slow, and the logs show which connections happened, not what was done inside them.

tips: Eliminate: B sits at the edge, away from the server, and D reviews connection logs weekly, too slow and too shallow.
Final two: C beats A because the host agent sees activity after decryption; a network sensor sees only encrypted packets.
Exam cue: when traffic is encrypted, monitor where it is decrypted: on the host itself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-94 Section 7.1.3 (Agent Locations: host agents see activity inside encrypted communications)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'host-based sensors see what encrypted traffic hides from network sensors' (notes 4.1.8 Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. AI in traffic monitoring
questions.question: A transit agency's AI traffic monitor learned its baseline over two weeks, and an incident review shows an intruder was active throughout. Which risk to the monitor should the security analyst rate GREATEST?

options.A: The intruder's traffic may now be scored as normal
options.B: The intruder's encrypted sessions stayed invisible to the model
options.C: Two weeks may miss monthly jobs, causing false alarms
options.D: The monitor will now flag all traffic as unusual

questions.key_concept: An anomaly model learns whatever it sees in training; if an attacker is active then, their behavior can become part of normal.
questions.pre_read: Weigh both facts in the stem before judging which effect matters most.
questions.correct_explanation: An AI monitor learns normal from its training traffic and flags what departs from it. If an intruder was active the whole time, their traffic is part of the baseline and may never be flagged. A training window too short for monthly jobs is the runner-up: it is a real flaw that causes false alarms, but false alarms get noticed, while a blind spot hides an active attacker.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption hides content. But models learn from timing, volume and destinations, which encryption leaves visible.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: two weeks can miss monthly or seasonal jobs. But that causes noisy false alarms, while a baseline containing the intruder silently hides them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the baseline is flawed. But a tainted baseline does not make everything look unusual; it makes the intruder's behavior look ordinary.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes models see nothing in encrypted traffic, and D reverses the effect; a tainted baseline makes intruder activity look normal rather than flagging it.
Final two: A beats C because a missed attacker is worse than extra alarms; false alarms get noticed, and learned blind spots do not.
Exam cue: an anomaly model's normal is only as clean as its training period. Train on trusted traffic, and retrain after a compromise.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-94 Section 2.3.2 (Anomaly-Based Detection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI monitors learn normal from training traffic, so an attacker present then can be learned as normal' (notes 4.1.9 AI in Traffic Monitoring, IDS and Firewalls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A furniture retailer's delivery drivers connect Bluetooth barcode scanners to their phones, and the network technician finds the scanners announce themselves to nearby devices all day. Which change is BEST?

options.A: Update the scanners' firmware on a regular schedule
options.B: Count on Bluetooth's short range to keep strangers away
options.C: Keep the scanners non-discoverable except while pairing
options.D: Require a screen-lock PIN on each driver's phone

questions.key_concept: Bluetooth devices should be discoverable only while pairing; staying discoverable invites unwanted pairing attempts.
questions.pre_read: Picture the scanners on a busy delivery day, then read each option in turn.
questions.correct_explanation: A discoverable device announces itself to anyone nearby and invites pairing attempts. Making the scanners discoverable only while pairing closes that exposure without stopping the drivers' work. Regular firmware updates are the runner-up because they fix known Bluetooth flaws and matter too, but they leave the scanners advertising themselves all day, which is the weakness found.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: firmware updates do fix Bluetooth flaws. But they leave the scanners advertising themselves all day, the weakness the technician actually found.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because Bluetooth reaches only a few meters. But antennas extend that range, and drivers work in busy public places where strangers are close.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it protects the phone. But a phone's screen lock does nothing to stop strangers finding and pairing with the discoverable scanners.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts short range, which antennas and crowds defeat, and D locks the phone but leaves the scanners open.
Final two: C beats A because it closes the weakness found; firmware updates help, but the scanners would still advertise all day.
Exam cue: match the fix to the finding. Bluetooth devices should be discoverable only while pairing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 Update 1 Section 4.4 (Bluetooth Security Checklist: undiscoverable except when pairing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'keep Bluetooth devices non-discoverable except while pairing' (notes 4.1.10 Wireless Security: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Key letter moved from B to C (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.question: A concert venue's ticketing website runs in its screened subnet and must save orders to a database on the internal network. Which change should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Join the web server to the internal network through a VPN tunnel
options.B: Allow all screened-subnet traffic into the internal network
options.C: Allow the whole screened subnet to reach the database port
options.D: Allow the web server alone to reach the database port

questions.key_concept: Servers in the screened subnet reach inside only on narrow paths: one server, to one system, on the one port needed.
questions.pre_read: For each rule, ask who else could use the path it opens.
questions.correct_explanation: The screened subnet holds the systems most exposed to attack, so any path inward must be as narrow as possible: only the web server, only to the database, only on the database port. Opening the database port to the whole screened subnet is the runner-up, but then any other server there, such as a mail gateway, gains a path to the order data.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a tunnel encrypts the link. But it joins an exposed server to the internal network, so an attacker who breaches it rides straight in.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it saves writing rules. But it lets any breached screened-subnet server into the internal network, defeating the screened subnet's purpose.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it limits traffic to the database port. But every other server in the screened subnet also gains a path to the order data.

tips: Eliminate: A tunnels an exposed server into the internal network, and B lets all screened-subnet traffic inside; both undo the screened subnet's purpose.
Final two: D beats C because only the web server needs the path; opening it to the whole subnet hands it to other exposed servers.
Exam cue: paths from the screened subnet inward should name one source, one destination and one port.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 3.1 (Network Layouts with Firewalls: public-facing servers on the DMZ); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7(5) (Boundary Protection | Deny by Default — Allow by Exception)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'screened-subnet servers reach inside only on narrow, approved paths' (notes 4.2.2 Firewall Zones and the Screened Subnet (DMZ)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: At a car dealership group, the admin pages of every switch and firewall can be reached from any employee's computer. Which change should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Turn off the switch ports that no one is using
options.B: Switch the admin pages from plain HTTP to HTTPS
options.C: Move the admin pages to a management VLAN for network staff only
options.D: Log every sign-in to the switch and firewall admin pages daily

questions.key_concept: Network device management belongs on a separate management VLAN that only network staff can reach.
questions.pre_read: Note who can reach the admin pages today, and what each option changes about that.
questions.correct_explanation: Admin pages control the whole network, so only the people who manage it should be able to reach them. A management VLAN, filtered so only network staff can connect, takes the pages out of every staff device's reach. Moving to HTTPS is the runner-up because it protects admin logins from eavesdropping, but every staff device could still reach and attack the pages.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because disabling unused ports is good hygiene. But it does not change who can reach the admin pages from active staff devices.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: HTTPS does stop admin logins being read in transit. But every staff device could still reach the pages and try to break in.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs help investigations. But logging records sign-ins after they happen; it does not stop staff devices reaching the pages.

tips: Eliminate: A tidies unused ports without changing who reaches the admin pages, and D records sign-ins without preventing access.
Final two: C beats B because it removes staff devices' path to the pages; HTTPS protects the login but leaves the pages reachable.
Exam cue: management interfaces belong on their own VLAN that only network staff can reach.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7(15) (Boundary Protection | Networked Privileged Accesses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'keep network management on its own VLAN reachable only by network staff' (notes 4.2.3 Virtual LANs (VLANs)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A game studio's operations team will micro-segment its 30 build and test servers, and the team lead asks a junior engineer to start. What should the engineer do FIRST?

options.A: Map the traffic each server actually sends and receives
options.B: Copy the perimeter firewall's rules onto every server
options.C: Buy a micro-segmentation product and turn on its defaults
options.D: Apply deny-all rules to every server, then fix what breaks

questions.key_concept: Micro-segmentation starts by mapping real traffic between workloads; rules written before mapping either break services or leave gaps.
questions.pre_read: Picture the studio's first week after each option is carried out.
questions.correct_explanation: Micro-segmentation rules allow each workload only the flows it needs, so the team must first learn what those flows are. Mapping real traffic gives the facts the rules are written from. Deny-all first is the runner-up because it is strict and secure on paper, but blocking blind breaks builds and tests, and fixing outages one by one invites rushed, overly broad allow rules.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because those rules are already approved. But perimeter rules describe traffic crossing the edge, not the flows between these servers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because tools help enforce policy. But default settings do not know which flows this studio's servers need; the rules still have to come from a map.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: deny by default is the end goal. But applying it before knowing the real flows breaks builds, and rushed fixes tend to open overly broad rules.

tips: Eliminate: B reuses edge rules that say nothing about traffic between servers, and C trusts defaults that know nothing of the studio's traffic.
Final two: A beats D because rules must rest on real flows; blocking first breaks work and invites broad fixes.
Exam cue: before writing segmentation rules, map the traffic; you cannot allow only what is needed until you know what is needed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 7.3 (Steps to Introducing ZTA to a Perimeter-Based Architected Network); NIST SP 800-215 Section 5.1 (Microsegmentation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'map real traffic first, then allow only the needed flows' (notes 4.2.4 Micro-Segmentation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust principles
questions.question: A vendor tells a water utility's IT manager that buying its access gateway will make the utility Zero Trust within a week. Which response from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Zero Trust only concerns traffic arriving from the internet
options.B: Zero Trust is a set of principles adopted in stages
options.C: With the gateway, network segmentation is no longer needed
options.D: The gateway is enough if it checks every user's identity

questions.key_concept: Zero Trust is a set of principles applied step by step across identity, devices, policy and monitoring, not a product bought once.
questions.pre_read: Read the vendor's promise closely before judging each response.
questions.correct_explanation: Zero Trust is a set of principles: verify identity, device health and need on every request, grant least privilege and assume breach. An organization adopts it in stages across identity, devices, policy and monitoring, so no single product delivers it in a week. Identity checks are the runner-up because they are central, but identity alone ignores device health, context and ongoing monitoring.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because outsiders are an obvious threat. But Zero Trust gives no trust to internal traffic either; requests from inside are checked just the same.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the gateway controls access. But a full Zero Trust design still includes segmentation; it moves boundaries closer to resources rather than removing them.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: identity checks are central to Zero Trust. But identity alone ignores device health, context and continued monitoring, which the principles also require.

tips: Eliminate: A limits Zero Trust to internet traffic, and C drops segmentation, which a full Zero Trust design still includes.
Final two: B beats D because Zero Trust needs identity, device, policy and monitoring together; one identity check is only part of it.
Exam cue: Zero Trust is a strategy adopted in stages; no single purchase delivers it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 7 (Migrating to a Zero Trust Architecture)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Zero Trust is a set of principles adopted in stages, not a product' (notes 4.2.6 Zero Trust Principles). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A recruitment agency's security analyst learns that its cloud servers run on physical hardware shared with other customers, each kept separate by the provider. Which essential cloud characteristic does this MOST accurately show?

options.A: Rapid elasticity
options.B: Resource pooling
options.C: Broad network access
options.D: Virtualization

questions.key_concept: Resource pooling means the provider serves many customers from shared hardware, assigning resources as needed while keeping customers apart.
questions.pre_read: Note exactly what is shared, and between whom, before matching a characteristic.
questions.correct_explanation: Resource pooling means the provider serves many customers from shared physical resources, assigning and reassigning them as demand changes, with each customer kept separate. Hardware shared across customers is exactly that. Rapid elasticity is the runner-up because pooling makes fast scaling possible, but elasticity describes one customer's capacity growing and shrinking with demand, not hardware shared among customers.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: pooling is what makes quick scaling possible. But elasticity is one customer's capacity growing and shrinking; sharing hardware among customers is pooling.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the servers are reached over a network. But broad network access means using services from many kinds of devices through standard methods.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because virtualization lets customers share hardware. But it is the technology that enables pooling, not one of the five essential characteristics.

tips: Eliminate: D is a technology, not one of the five characteristics, and C is about reaching services from many kinds of devices.
Final two: B beats A because sharing hardware among customers is pooling; elasticity is one customer's capacity tracking demand.
Exam cue: shared hardware is pooling, scaling with demand is elasticity, and virtualization is the tool underneath, not a characteristic.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: essential characteristics)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'shared hardware among customers is resource pooling, which virtualization enables' (notes 4.3.1 The Five Essential Characteristics of Cloud Computing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Key letter moved from D to B (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.question: A small theater company wants email and shared calendars online without running or patching any servers or programs itself. Which service model should its IT volunteer choose as BEST?

options.A: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
options.B: Software as a service (SaaS)
options.C: Platform as a service (PaaS)
options.D: A private cloud deployment

questions.key_concept: In SaaS the provider runs the whole application; the customer still manages its users, settings and data.
questions.pre_read: List what the company is willing to manage itself, then match a model to that list.
questions.correct_explanation: SaaS delivers a finished application, such as email and calendars, that the provider runs and patches from top to bottom. The theater company then manages only its users, settings and data. PaaS is the runner-up because the provider manages a lot there too, but the customer must still deploy its own application on the platform and look after it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is flexible. But IaaS leaves the customer running and patching operating systems and software, the very work the company wants to avoid.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: PaaS does hand the operating system and runtime to the provider. But the company would still have to deploy and maintain its own email application.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it sounds safe and simple. But it names a deployment model, not a service model, and a private cloud usually means more work, not less.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves the company patching servers, and D names a deployment model, not a service model.
Final two: B beats C because SaaS delivers the finished application; with PaaS the company would still run its own email software.
Exam cue: the less the customer wants to run, the higher up the stack: IaaS, then PaaS, then SaaS. Users and data always stay with the customer.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'match the service model to what the customer will still run' (notes 4.3.3 Cloud Service Models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Key letter moved from C to B (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.question: A food delivery startup runs its order system on infrastructure as a service (IaaS) virtual machines, and the hypervisor beneath them has a critical flaw. Who is MOST responsible for applying the hypervisor patch?

options.A: The provider, which runs the physical host servers
options.B: The startup's server team, which manages the virtual machines
options.C: The startup's developers, who wrote the order system
options.D: The hypervisor's maker, which releases fixes for its flaws

questions.key_concept: In every service model the provider secures the physical hosts and virtualization layer; in IaaS the customer starts at the guest operating system.
questions.pre_read: Draw the layers from the hardware up, and mark who manages each one in IaaS.
questions.correct_explanation: In IaaS the customer controls the guest operating systems and everything on them, but the provider runs the hardware and the hypervisor underneath. So the provider must patch this flaw. The startup's server team is the runner-up because in IaaS it patches a lot, including the virtual machines' operating systems, but it has no control over the hypervisor itself.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: in IaaS the server team patches the virtual machines' operating systems. But the hypervisor sits beneath them, on the provider's side of the line.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because developers fix flaws in code. But the order system is application code; the hypervisor is infrastructure the startup cannot touch.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the maker writes the fix. But releasing a patch is not applying it; the provider, which runs the hypervisor on its hosts, must install it.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses application code with infrastructure, and D confuses releasing a fix with applying it.
Final two: A beats B because the provider runs the host servers and the hypervisor on them; the customer's IaaS duties start at the guest operating system.
Exam cue: the provider always secures the hardware and virtualization layer. In IaaS, the customer's share starts at the guest operating system.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models); NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.6 (Software Isolation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the provider secures the virtualization layer and the IaaS customer starts at the guest operating system' (notes 4.3.5 The Shared Responsibility Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): stem no longer names who runs the hypervisor. Cross-review fix (31 Oct 2026): IaaS spelled out at first use in the stem (CD-32). Fix-up round 1 (31 Oct 2026): the stem asks who applies the patch, as cc_d4_016 does, so the maker that writes it is not a foothold. Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026): the Final two tip now links the provider's host servers to the hypervisor that runs on them; options unchanged.

questions.question: A payroll firm's procedure lets its junior engineer fix baseline failures that cloud security posture management (CSPM) finds; one is a test server with SSH open to the internet. What should the engineer do FIRST?

options.A: Open a ticket asking the cloud provider to fix the setting
options.B: Restrict SSH to the admin team's addresses and record the change
options.C: Report the SSH exposure to the server's owner and await a decision
options.D: Accept the finding as low risk for a test server

questions.key_concept: When a procedure assigns you a fix, make it and record it; access settings on a customer's own cloud servers are the customer's job.
questions.pre_read: Picture the test server's next few hours under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedure gives the engineer authority to fix findings that break the baseline, so this is a pre-approved change: the engineer restricts SSH to the approved admin addresses now and records the change. Reporting to the server's owner is the runner-up: escalation suits decisions outside one's role, but here the procedure assigns the fix, and waiting leaves SSH open to the internet.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the server runs on the provider's platform. But who may reach the customer's own servers is a customer setting; the provider will not change it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: owners decide on changes outside the procedure. But this fix is assigned to the engineer, and waiting leaves SSH exposed to the internet.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because test servers seem low value. But accepting risk is the owner's call, not the engineer's, and attackers scan the internet for open SSH on any server.

tips: Eliminate: A hands a customer setting to the provider, and D treats a test server as safe to expose.
Final two: B beats C because the procedure assigns this fix to the engineer; escalating a task you own only prolongs the exposure.
Exam cue: escalate what is outside your authority, and act on what the procedure assigns to you.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'CSPM compares settings to a baseline; fix assigned drift promptly because cloud settings are the customer's' (notes 4.3.8 Cloud Misconfiguration, CSPM and CASB). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): framed as a pre-approved change so it agrees with the change-control items in D2 and D5. Cross-review fix (31 Oct 2026): CSPM spelled out at first use in the stem (CD-32); runner-up C now names the SSH exposure, so the key is no longer the only option echoing the stem's SSH or the longest option (CD-14); relabeled application, since one stated fact (the procedure assigns the fix) decides it (CD-21).

questions.question: A travel insurer fine-tuned a language model on customer claim emails using a cloud AI service, and a developer wants to publish it openly. Which advice from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Publish it once the original claim emails are deleted
options.B: Publish it, since a model stores only numeric weights
options.C: Let the cloud provider decide, since it hosts the tuned model
options.D: Keep it private, since it can leak details from the claims

questions.key_concept: A model tuned on sensitive data can leak that data, so it needs the same protection as the data it learned from.
questions.pre_read: Picture a stranger downloading the published model and trying it out.
questions.correct_explanation: Models can memorize parts of their training data, and researchers have drawn email addresses, phone numbers and locations out of language models by prompting them. A model tuned on claim emails may therefore reveal customers' details, so it needs the same protection as the emails. Deleting the original emails is the runner-up because it removes the source, but the tuned model keeps what it learned.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: deleting the source emails does remove one copy of the data. But the tuned model keeps what it learned, so it can still reveal details.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because model files are numeric weights. But those weights can encode memorized training text that the right prompts draw back out.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model sits on the provider's platform. But the tuned model is the customer's asset, and the customer decides how it is shared.

tips: Eliminate: B treats model weights as harmless numbers, and C hands the customer's sharing decision to the provider.
Final two: D beats A because the tuned model carries what it learned; deleting the source emails does not remove it from the model.
Exam cue: a model trained on sensitive data inherits that data's sensitivity. Protect it like the data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 3.3.2 (Information Extraction: leaking sensitive training data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a tuned model carries patterns from its training data and needs the same protection' (notes 4.3.9 Shared Responsibility for AI Workloads). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): scenario changed away from the notes 4.3.9 worked example; explanation matches the source's examples of leaked details.

questions.question: Guests' phones on an aquarium's visitor Wi-Fi have working IP addresses and can open the ticket site by its IP address, but not by its name. What should the network technician check FIRST?

options.A: The switch and its MAC address table
options.B: The DNS server and its records
options.C: The DHCP server and its leases
options.D: The router and its routing table

questions.key_concept: DHCP gives each device its address and settings; DNS turns the names people type into the IP addresses networks use.
questions.pre_read: Picture each step a phone takes between typing a web address and loading the page.
questions.correct_explanation: The phones have working addresses and reach the site by IP address, so the switch and router are doing their jobs. What fails is turning the site's name into its address, which is the job of DNS, so the technician checks DNS first. DHCP is the runner-up because it tells devices which DNS server to use and can be the root cause, but the failing step is the name lookup, so DHCP comes second.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because switches carry every local frame. But reaching the site by IP address proves frames are moving, and a switch never deals with names.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: DHCP tells phones which DNS server to ask, so it can cause this. But the failing step is the name lookup, so check DNS first, then DHCP.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because routers carry traffic out to the internet. But the site loads by IP address, so routing works; only lookups by name fail.

tips: Eliminate: A and D fall away because the site loads by IP address, which proves frames are switched and packets are routed.
Final two: B beats C because the failing step is the name lookup; check DNS first, and look at DHCP only if the phones are sent to the wrong DNS server.
Exam cue: works by IP address but not by name? Think DNS. No address at all? Think DHCP.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-81 Rev. 3 Section 1.1 (Domain Name Systems: translating domain names into IP addresses is called name resolution)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'DHCP hands out IP addresses; DNS turns names into IP addresses' (notes 4.1.1 Network Building Blocks). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Audit fix-up (31 Oct 2026): options are now short labels without definitions, so the item tests what each service does rather than matching the stem to a definition.

questions.question: A taxi dispatch firm's network technician wants all UDP ports blocked at the office firewall because UDP lacks delivery checks. Which approach should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Block every UDP port at the firewall
options.B: Allow only the UDP ports that services need
options.C: Allow outgoing UDP traffic but block incoming UDP
options.D: Carry the services staff need over TCP's encrypted sessions

questions.key_concept: UDP skips delivery checks for speed; that is not a security flaw. Allow the UDP ports needed services use, and deny the rest.
questions.pre_read: Think about which everyday services would stop if a whole protocol were switched off.
questions.correct_explanation: UDP trades delivery checks for speed, which suits name lookups, clock sync and live voice; it is not a security flaw. The right control is the usual one: allow the UDP ports the firm's services need and deny everything else. Blocking all UDP is the runner-up because it looks cautious, but services such as DNS name lookups and clock sync normally run over UDP, so the office would break without removing a real risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: denying by default is sound. But everyday services such as DNS name lookups and clock sync normally use UDP, so blocking every UDP port breaks them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because most attacks seem to arrive from outside. But malware inside can send data out over any open UDP port, so ports no service needs stay closed both ways.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because TCP sounds more reliable. But TCP adds delivery checks, not encryption, so moving services to it does not secure them.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves every outgoing UDP port open for malware to send data out, and D mistakes TCP's delivery checks for encryption.
Final two: B beats A because UDP's missing delivery checks are a design choice, not a weakness; close only the ports no service needs.
Exam cue: filter by service, not by protocol. Open exactly the ports a needed service uses, whether TCP or UDP.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7(5) (Boundary Protection | Deny by Default — Allow by Exception); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-7 (Least Functionality)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'UDP skips delivery checks and is not insecure in itself; firewalls filter on protocol and port' (notes 4.1.3 The TCP/IP Model, TCP and UDP). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): C is now a partial outbound-only rule instead of the opposite extreme of A, so the key no longer sits between two absolutes. Cross-domain gate (31 Oct 2026): D now also names the services staff need, so 'need' no longer sits on the key alone.

questions.question: A shoe retailer's owner says its card terminals are safe because they use private 192.168.x.x addresses, which the internet does not route. Which reply from the network technician is MOST accurate?

options.A: Firewall rules still decide what traffic reaches the terminals
options.B: Address translation on the router already works as a firewall
options.C: Private addresses encrypt the terminals' traffic to the bank
options.D: Switching to IPv6 would make the terminals secure by default

questions.key_concept: Private addresses and address translation hide devices but filter nothing; firewall rules and segmentation still decide what reaches them.
questions.pre_read: Picture the different paths by which harmful traffic could reach a card terminal.
questions.correct_explanation: Private ranges are simply not routed on the internet; they block nothing themselves. Malware on a staff computer, a phishing click or an allowed port can still reach the terminals, so firewall rules and segmentation do the protecting. Address translation is the runner-up because it stops outsiders starting connections, but NIST treats it as routing, not a firewall feature, and it filters nothing inside the network.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: translation does stop outsiders starting connections inward. But NIST classes it as routing, not firewalling, and it filters nothing already inside.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because private sounds like protected. But an address only says where traffic goes; encryption comes from protocols such as TLS.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because IPv6 was designed with IPsec in mind. But someone must still set IPsec up; a newer protocol version is not secure by default.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses an address range with encryption, and D assumes IPv6 arrives with its security already switched on.
Final two: A beats B because address translation is routing, not filtering; only rules decide which traffic reaches the terminals.
Exam cue: hiding an address is not filtering traffic. Look for the control that actually decides what gets through.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 3.2 (Firewalls Acting as Network Address Translators: NAT is not part of a firewall's security functionality)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'private addresses are not a security control; they hide addresses but filter nothing' (notes 4.1.4 IPv4 and IPv6). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A landscaping firm's remote staff find the VPN slow, and the IT manager proposes split tunneling so only company traffic uses it. Which assessment from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Company traffic would cross the internet without encryption
options.B: It would lower risk, since less traffic crosses the tunnel
options.C: Web browsing would bypass company filtering and monitoring
options.D: Staff could sign in to the VPN without multifactor authentication

questions.key_concept: A VPN protects only the traffic sent through it; split tunneling sends all other traffic around the company's filtering and monitoring.
questions.pre_read: Follow a staff member's traffic under each tunneling choice.
questions.correct_explanation: With split tunneling, only company traffic enters the tunnel; everything else goes straight to the internet, where the firm can no longer filter or monitor it, and NIST advises considering disabling it on untrusted networks. Lower risk from less tunnel traffic is the runner-up because it sounds efficient, but it saves bandwidth, not risk: traffic that leaves the tunnel loses the company's protection.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because some traffic leaves the tunnel. But split tunneling still sends company traffic through the encrypted tunnel; only other traffic goes direct.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: split tunneling does cut the load on the VPN. But that saves bandwidth, not risk; traffic outside the tunnel loses company filtering and monitoring.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both settings live on the VPN. But tunneling mode and sign-in are separate; multifactor authentication stays required either way.

tips: Eliminate: A forgets that company traffic still uses the tunnel, and D mixes up the tunneling mode with how users sign in.
Final two: C beats B because less tunnel traffic saves bandwidth, not risk; traffic sent around the tunnel loses the firm's protections.
Exam cue: a VPN protects only what passes through it. Ask what traffic a design sends around the company's controls.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-46 Rev. 2 Section 3.3.3 (Access Control for Network Communications: split tunneling stops the organization examining much of the traffic)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'split tunneling sends non-company traffic around company filtering and monitoring' (notes 4.1.6 Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. Embedded and control systems
questions.question: A glass factory's security analyst, with no rights on the control network its engineers own, sees an unknown device sending commands to the furnace controllers as temperatures climb. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Block the device at the control firewall, then tell the engineers
options.B: Power off the furnace controllers from the server room
options.C: Actively scan the furnace network to find the device
options.D: Alert the control room operators and the control engineers

questions.key_concept: In OT, operators bring a running process to a safe state; security staff alert them and the system's engineers rather than act on the controls.
questions.pre_read: Think about what could happen on the factory floor in the next few minutes.
questions.correct_explanation: Climbing furnace temperatures can hurt people, and in operational technology human safety comes first. The control room operators can bring the furnace to a safe state by procedure, and the control engineers own the control network, so the analyst alerts both at once. Blocking the device is the runner-up because it targets the cause, but the analyst has no rights to change the control firewall, and a block does not cool an overheating furnace.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: blocking and telling the owners both matter. But the analyst has no rights on the control network, and a block does not make the overheating furnace safe.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because stopping the controllers seems to stop the danger. But cutting power to a running furnace's controls can itself be unsafe; operators make it safe by procedure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a scan would find the device fast. But active scans can freeze fragile controllers, adding risk to a process already in trouble.

tips: Eliminate: B cuts power to controls the operators need to make the furnace safe, and C actively scans controllers that such scans can freeze.
Final two: D beats A because the operators can make the furnace safe now and the engineers own the firewall change; blocking it yourself oversteps and leaves the heat climbing.
Exam cue: in OT, the operators who run the process bring it to a safe state. Security staff alert them and the system's engineers at once, then contain through the incident process.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 2.4 (Comparing OT and IT System Security: human safety is paramount, followed by protection of the process); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MA-04 (incidents are escalated or elevated as needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'with systems that move physical things, protect people first, then keep the process running' (notes 4.1.11 Embedded Systems and Industrial Control Systems). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026): the stem says the control engineers own the control network, and A now also tells the engineers, so the key no longer stands out as the only owner-naming, two-party option.

questions.question: A gym chain's facilities manager owns its new door cameras, which all ship with the same default password; device hardening is the network technician's step in the setup procedure. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Give each camera its own unique password, then connect it
options.B: Connect them as shipped, relying on the edge firewall
options.C: Report the default passwords to the facilities manager
options.D: Keep the default but disable remote access on each camera

questions.key_concept: Default passwords are among the first things attackers try; when the setup procedure assigns the change, make it before the device connects.
questions.pre_read: Picture the first hour each camera spends on the network under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: A shared default password is published and among the first things attackers try, so each camera needs its own before it connects. Device hardening is the technician's step in the setup procedure, so they set each camera's own password now. Reporting to the facilities manager is the runner-up because the manager owns the cameras, but the procedure gives this step to the technician, so reporting and waiting only leaves the published default in place longer.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the edge firewall blocks outside connections. But a compromised device inside can still reach the cameras, and default passwords are tried first.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the facilities manager owns the cameras and decides how they are used. But the procedure gives hardening to the technician, so reporting and waiting only delays the fix.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because closing remote access shuts one path in. But anyone on the inside network can still log in with the published default, so it must still be replaced.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts the edge firewall to protect devices inside, and D leaves the published default in place for anyone already inside.
Final two: A beats C because the procedure gives this step to the technician; owners decide what falls outside the procedure, not the steps it assigns.
Exam cue: check the procedure before the org chart. A step it gives you is yours to do; the owner decides what it does not cover.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management); NIST SP 800-213 Section 2.3 (How IoT Devices May Create Security Challenges)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'change default passwords at installation' (notes 4.1.12 Internet of Things (IoT) Security). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): stem wording varied from the fixed 'the procedure assigns' clause, C reworded from Ask to Report (bank-wide Report/Ask tell), new exam cue.

questions.question: A home builder's sales office runs staff computers, guest Wi-Fi and a payment terminal for deposits on one flat network. Which basis for dividing them into segments should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: By IP address order, filling each subnet in turn
options.B: By office floor, so each floor's devices share one segment
options.C: By device type, so like devices share the same rules
options.D: By trust level and purpose, so rules fit each group

questions.key_concept: Segments group systems that share a trust level and purpose, so rules between them can allow only the traffic each group needs.
questions.pre_read: Picture which devices would end up sharing a segment under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Segmentation works by putting systems with the same trust level and job together, then allowing only needed traffic between groups. Guests, staff computers and payment systems need very different protection, so they belong apart. Grouping by device type is the runner-up because similar devices often get similar settings, but a guest's laptop and a staff laptop are the same type with very different trust, so they would share a segment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because subnets are often filled this way. But address order says nothing about risk, and subnets without rules between them are not real segments.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because floors give a neat physical layout. But one floor mixes guests, staff and payment systems, so its segment would join devices needing very different protection.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: similar devices often need similar settings. But a guest's laptop and a staff laptop are the same type with very different trust, so they would share a segment.

tips: Eliminate: A groups by address order, which says nothing about risk, and B groups by floor, which puts guest and payment devices side by side.
Final two: D beats C because segment rules depend on trust and purpose; grouping by type would put a guest's laptop beside a staff laptop.
Exam cue: group by trust and purpose, then filter between the groups. Floor, address range or device type help only where they match trust.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7(21) (Boundary Protection | Isolation of System Components)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'systems are grouped by trust level and purpose, with controls on the traffic between them' (notes 4.2.1 Network Segmentation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026): C no longer echoes the stem's 'systems' and now carries a reason clause like the other options. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): the stem now names the staff, guest and payment devices the explanations argue from, and the pre-read no longer echoes the key. Audit fix-up (31 Oct 2026): D (device maker) was a strawman; it is now grouping by device type, a plausible rival with its own rules clause, and the tips and explanations name D as the runner-up. Key letter moved from C to D (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Defense in depth
questions.question: A phone carrier's chatbot runs on a vendor's AI model with built-in content filters, and the product lead calls that enough. Which addition should the security analyst propose to BEST apply defense in depth?

options.A: Keep the vendor and model names out of public view
options.B: Upgrade to the vendor's stricter filters and log what they block
options.C: Add an edge firewall rule to block harmful chatbot replies
options.D: Check and log each chatbot reply before customers see it

questions.key_concept: Defense in depth adds a different kind of control at another point, such as checking replies before release; stricter vendor filters are still one layer.
questions.pre_read: Imagine someone tricks the vendor's filters with a clever prompt, and follow the reply.
questions.correct_explanation: Defense in depth needs layers that fail independently. The carrier's own reply check sits outside the vendor's model, so it can catch a bad reply the vendor's filters miss. NIST warns that checkers can share blind spots with the model, so the logs let staff spot misuse that gets past both. Upgrading to the vendor's stricter filters is the runner-up, but one trick may beat both, and their log shows only what they caught.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because secrecy can slow attackers a little. But anyone can still type tricky prompts into the chatbot, so hiding names cannot catch a harmful reply.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: stricter filters do improve that layer. But they are still the vendor's filters, so one trick could defeat both, and logging what they block shows nothing they miss.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because firewalls are a classic layer. But an edge firewall filters network traffic, not what a chatbot says inside allowed web sessions.

tips: Eliminate: C expects a network firewall rule to judge chatbot content, and A relies on secrecy, which cannot catch a harmful reply.
Final two: D beats B because the carrier's own check is a separate layer it controls; stricter vendor filters can be fooled the same way, and their log shows only what they caught.
Exam cue: a stronger version of the same control adds no depth; add a control of another kind at another point.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-8(1) (Security and Privacy Architectures | Defense in Depth); NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 3.3.3 (Mitigations: output detection and activity monitoring add defense in depth, but detectors may fail together with the model they check)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'each layer should fail independently, and AI systems get layers too, including filtering and monitoring of outputs' (notes 4.2.5 Defense in Depth). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): A loses its reason clause and C is now a real (wrong-layer) addition; the explanation ties the NIST correlated-failure point to the logs and separates an added layer from limiting access. Audit fix-up (31 Oct 2026): correct explanation rewritten in plain steps; the absolute closing line about limiting access is removed. Cross-domain gate (31 Oct 2026): B gains a same-form log clause so oversight wording is not on the key alone; key_concept and exam cue re-angled away from cc_d4_027's 'fail independently' wording.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust components
questions.question: A record label is replacing its VPN with Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) for remote staff. Which difference should the network technician explain as MOST important?

options.A: Each verified user reaches only the specific apps they need
options.B: All traffic between staff and company systems becomes encrypted
options.C: Staff on company laptops no longer need to sign in
options.D: The office firewall and internal segments can be retired

questions.key_concept: A VPN places a user on the network; Zero Trust Network Access connects a verified user to specific applications, one session at a time.
questions.pre_read: Picture what a remote staff member can reach right after connecting, under each approach.
questions.correct_explanation: A VPN puts remote users on the internal network, where they can often reach far more than they need. ZTNA connects each verified user only to the applications they are allowed, one session at a time, and keeps checking. Encryption is the runner-up because ZTNA does encrypt traffic, but the VPN already did that, so encryption is not what changes.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: ZTNA does encrypt traffic in transit. But the VPN already did, so encryption is not the difference; the change is what each user can reach.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because company laptops are trusted assets. But Zero Trust grants nothing for owning a device or for its location; every user still signs in.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because ZTNA moves checks to each application. But Zero Trust adds to firewalls and segmentation; it does not replace the network controls behind it.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts a device because the company owns it, and D assumes ZTNA replaces the firewall and segments behind it.
Final two: A beats B because VPNs and ZTNA both encrypt; what ZTNA changes is access to specific apps instead of the whole network.
Exam cue: a VPN connects you to a network; Zero Trust connects a verified user to a resource. Look for per-app, per-session access.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 2.1 (Tenets of Zero Trust)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Zero Trust Network Access connects a verified user to one application and keeps checking; a VPN places the user on the network' (notes 4.2.7 Zero Trust Architecture Components). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): role changed to the canonical network technician (rule 11).

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Network access control
questions.question: At a convention center, a new digital sign cannot do the 802.1X sign-in that network access control (NAC) requires, and NAC exceptions need the policy owner's approval. What should the network technician do FIRST?

options.A: Admit the sign by its MAC address, which proves its identity
options.B: Ask the NAC policy owner to decide on the sign's access
options.C: Turn off NAC on the sign's port, then tell the policy owner
options.D: Block the sign until it can do the 802.1X sign-in

questions.key_concept: Devices that cannot meet NAC get limited access through an exception the policy owner approves and records, never through a quiet bypass.
questions.pre_read: Picture the sign's network port tomorrow under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: The sign cannot use the normal NAC sign-in, so it needs an exception, and exceptions need the policy owner's approval. The technician sends the request; the owner can approve limited, profiled access that is recorded and time-limited. Turning off NAC first is the runner-up because the sign works sooner and the owner still hears of it, but it makes the owner's decision for them and leaves the port open to any device.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a MAC address identifies a network card. But MAC addresses are easy to copy, so one proves nothing about which device is connecting.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the owner is told, and the sign works sooner. But switching NAC off makes the exception decision for the owner and leaves the port open to anyone.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the sign fails the standard check. But a sign may never gain 802.1X; NAC designs give such devices limited access through an approved exception.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts an easily copied MAC address, and D treats NAC as a ban rather than a way to grant fitting access.
Final two: B beats C because exceptions belong to the policy owner; turning off the check first, even with a report afterward, decides for them.
Exam cue: when a device cannot meet a control, route the exception to its owner. Never bypass the control and report it afterward.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.7 (Network Access Control: health checks and limited access for remediation); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'devices that cannot use 802.1X get limited access, and exceptions go to the policy owner' (notes 4.2.8 Network Access Control (NAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. AI development environments
questions.question: A card issuer's fraud model retrains nightly on a dataset that every developer account can edit, because its AI development segment is treated as trusted. Which control should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Isolate the segment further from the office network
options.B: Scan the dataset for malware and log each nightly retraining run
options.C: Restrict edits to approved data engineers and log every change
options.D: Encrypt the dataset so that edits cannot alter the model

questions.key_concept: Training data shapes what a model learns, so only named people should change it, and every change should be logged.
questions.pre_read: Picture one careless or hostile edit to the dataset, and follow it into tomorrow's model.
questions.correct_explanation: Whoever can edit training data can quietly change what the model learns, for example teaching it to wave through one kind of fraud. So edits go only to approved people who need them, and every change is logged so bad records can be traced and removed. Malware scanning is the runner-up, but poisoned records are ordinary-looking data, not malicious code, and a retraining log does not show who changed a record.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because segmenting AI work is good practice. But the risk is already inside: every developer account can edit the data, and a tighter wall does not change that.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: checking data before training is wise. But poisoned records look like normal transactions, so a malware scan passes them, and a retraining log omits who changed a record.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption protects data. But it stops outsiders reading files; anyone allowed to edit the dataset can still change what the model learns.

tips: Eliminate: D expects encryption to stop people who are allowed to edit, and A adds a wall around a segment whose risk is already inside it.
Final two: C beats B because poisoned records are ordinary data that malware scans pass; limiting and logging each edit prevents and traces them, which a retraining log cannot.
Exam cue: being inside an AI development segment grants no trust. Under Zero Trust, each change to training data needs a named, least-privilege identity and a log.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 2.3.2 (Targeted Poisoning); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'training data gets Zero Trust treatment, named users with least privilege and a log of every change, because tampering can poison the model' (notes 4.2.9 Segmenting AI Development Environments). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): re-angled to Zero Trust inside the AI segment (4.2.9): the stem says the segment is treated as trusted, A is a plain network-isolation distractor without a reason clause, new exam cue. Cross-domain gate (31 Oct 2026): B gains a same-form log clause so oversight wording is not on the key alone.

questions.question: A fitness app company moves its payment logic to serverless functions, and a developer says the company now has nothing left to secure. Which duty MOST clearly stays with the company?

options.A: Hardening the hypervisor on the provider's physical host servers
options.B: Patching the operating system underneath the running functions
options.C: Encrypting the provider's links between its data centers
options.D: Limiting each function's permissions and its stored secrets

questions.key_concept: Serverless hands the servers to the provider, but the customer still owns each function's code, permissions, secrets and data.
questions.pre_read: List what the company writes and configures itself when it deploys a function.
questions.correct_explanation: In serverless computing the provider runs and patches everything under the code, but the company still writes the functions and decides what each may do. Over-broad permissions or exposed secrets in a payment function are the company's risk. Patching the operating system is the runner-up because customers do that in IaaS, but with serverless the provider manages the servers and their operating systems.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because hypervisors isolate workloads. But the provider secures the hypervisor and physical hosts in every cloud service model.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: customers patch guest operating systems in IaaS. But with serverless the provider manages the servers underneath, including their operating systems.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption in transit matters. But the provider's own network between its data centers is the provider's to secure.

tips: Eliminate: A and C are the provider's own infrastructure in every service model, so they never move to the customer.
Final two: D beats B because serverless hands the servers and their operating systems to the provider; code, permissions and secrets stay with the customer.
Exam cue: however much the provider runs, the customer keeps its code, identities, permissions and data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'serverless leaves the customer owning the function's code, permissions, secrets and data' (notes 4.3.2 Virtualization and Containers in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A botanical garden keeps its plant records database in a private cloud and its public website on a public cloud, linked for exhibit data. Which deployment model should its IT manager record as MOST accurate?

options.A: Public cloud
options.B: Multi-cloud
options.C: Community cloud
options.D: Hybrid cloud

questions.key_concept: A hybrid cloud joins two or more deployment models, such as private and public; using several providers is called multi-cloud.
questions.pre_read: List where each of the garden's systems runs and how the two are linked.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST defines a hybrid cloud as two or more distinct cloud infrastructures, such as private and public, bound together so data and applications can move between them. The garden joins a private cloud to a public one, so it is hybrid, and the link between them needs securing. Multi-cloud is the runner-up because two clouds are involved, but the term means using several providers, which may all be public.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the website runs on a public cloud. But the records database sits in a private cloud, so the whole setup is not public.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: two clouds are in use. But multi-cloud means using several providers; joining a private cloud to a public one is a hybrid of two models.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the setup links clouds together. But a community cloud is built for several organizations with shared needs, not for one garden.

tips: Eliminate: C needs several organizations with shared needs, and A would fit only if every part ran on a public cloud.
Final two: D beats B because the setup mixes two deployment models; multi-cloud is about using several providers.
Exam cue: hybrid mixes models (private plus public); multi-cloud mixes providers. Count models first, then providers.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: deployment models)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a hybrid cloud joins two or more models, and the links between them must be secured' (notes 4.3.4 Cloud Deployment Models). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.3 Cloud security. Cloud roles and agreements
questions.question: An e-sports league's cloud contract promises 99.95% uptime, and its manager says the league therefore needs no plan for provider outages. Which reply from the continuity coordinator is MOST accurate?

options.A: That target still allows about four hours of outage a year
options.B: Service credits in the contract will make up for any outage
options.C: The provider's ISO/IEC 27001 certificate covers outage planning
options.D: The provider's backups stop outages from affecting the league

questions.key_concept: A service level agreement sets an availability target and a remedy such as service credits; outages still happen, so continuity plans must cover them.
questions.pre_read: Picture the league's biggest match night falling inside an outage.
questions.correct_explanation: An uptime figure is a target, not a promise of no outages: NIST notes that 99.95% still means about 4.4 hours of downtime a year, and scheduled maintenance is often excluded. Availability must be covered in continuity planning. Service credits are the runner-up because the contract does offer a remedy, but credits usually refund part of the fee, not the league's lost matches or income.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: service level agreements do offer credits when targets are missed. But credits usually refund part of the fee; they do not restore lost matches or income.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a certificate shows strong provider controls. But it covers the provider's own scope, not the league's plans for when a service is down.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because backups protect the league's data. But backups restore data after a loss; they do not keep the service running while the provider is down.

tips: Eliminate: D confuses backups, which restore data, with keeping the service running, and C stretches a provider's certificate over the customer's own planning.
Final two: A beats B because an agreement's remedy is usually a partial refund; the outage still happens, so the league must plan for it.
Exam cue: a service level agreement sets a target and a remedy, not a guarantee. Keep continuity plans for the hours it still allows.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.8 (Availability: 99.95% availability still means about 4.38 hours of downtime a year)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the service level agreement sets a target, such as 99.9% availability, and a remedy; outages still happen' (notes 4.3.6 Cloud Roles and Agreements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Audit fix-up (31 Oct 2026): D was the mirror of the key ('a few seconds' against 'about four hours'); it is now the backups-equal-availability misconception, so no opposite pair points to the key.

questions.question: After moving its case files, a legal-aid charity is leaving a cloud service that stored them encrypted under keys the charity manages. What should its system administrator do to BEST make every remaining copy unreadable?

options.A: Re-encrypt the files under new keys before deleting them
options.B: Destroy the encryption keys that protect the files
options.C: Delete every case file and its old encrypted versions
options.D: Cancel the subscription so the provider erases the disks

questions.key_concept: Customers cannot wipe a cloud provider's disks; destroying the encryption keys they control makes every remaining copy unreadable.
questions.pre_read: Think about where copies of a cloud file live besides the folder you can see.
questions.correct_explanation: Cloud data sits in replicas and backups the charity cannot reach, and it cannot wipe the provider's disks. Because the files are encrypted with keys the charity controls, destroying those keys makes every copy unreadable; NIST notes that this cryptographic erase may be the only workable purge for cloud storage. Deleting the files is the runner-up because it clears what the charity sees, but replicas and backups remain.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fresh keys feel safer. But older replicas and backups stay encrypted under the old keys, which still exist and can still decrypt them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: deleting files and old versions removes the copies the charity can see. But replicas and provider backups can stay readable for some time.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because providers do remove data after an account closes. But the timing and method are the provider's, and the charity cannot verify them.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves the old keys able to read older copies, and D leaves the job to the provider's own timing.
Final two: B beats C because deleting leaves replicas and backups behind; destroying the keys makes every copy unreadable at once.
Exam cue: for data you cannot physically reach, destroying the keys you control is how you make every copy unreadable.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 Section 3.1.2 (Purge Sanitization Method: for cloud storage, cryptographic erase may be the only viable purge technique); NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.7 (Data Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'at exit, customers cannot wipe the provider's disks, so they delete data and destroy its keys' (notes 4.3.7 Protecting Data in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Audit fix-up (31 Oct 2026): the stem now says the files were moved first, so destroying the keys loses nothing the charity must keep, and uses the canonical role 'system administrator'; B no longer echoes the stem's 'stored'.

questions.question: A parking garage operator's switches answer SNMPv2c monitoring queries using the community string 'public', and the network lead approves all switch changes. What should the junior network technician do FIRST?

options.A: Move SNMP to an unusual port so scanners miss it
options.B: Change the community string from 'public' to 'private'
options.C: Ask the network lead to approve moving the switches to SNMPv3
options.D: Move every switch to SNMPv3 tonight, then tell the network lead

questions.key_concept: SNMP versions 1 and 2c send community strings in cleartext; SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption. Device changes go through whoever approves them.
questions.pre_read: Picture what an eavesdropper on the network sees during each monitoring query.
questions.correct_explanation: SNMPv2c sends its community string, in effect a password, in cleartext, and 'public' is a well-known default, so SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption is the right fix. The network lead approves switch changes, so the technician asks the lead to approve the move to SNMPv3. Changing every switch tonight is the runner-up because it applies the right fix, but doing it without approval bypasses change control and risks breaking monitoring.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because an odd port looks hidden. But scanners find services on any port, and the community string still crosses the network in cleartext.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes the default value. But 'private' is another well-known default, and SNMPv2c still sends it in cleartext.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: SNMPv3 is the right protocol. But the network lead approves switch changes, and an unapproved change across every switch could break monitoring or the network.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on an unusual port, and B swaps one well-known, cleartext community string for another.
Final two: C beats D because the network lead approves switch changes; even the right fix goes through the person who approves it.
Exam cue: pick the encrypted version of the protocol (SNMPv3, SSH, SFTP), then route the change through whoever approves it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-8(1) (Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity | Cryptographic Protection); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
