questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-125 Section 2.2 (Types of Full Virtualization: a bare metal hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, while a hosted hypervisor runs on top of the host OS)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, as in cloud data centers; a Type 2 hypervisor runs on an ordinary operating system' (notes 4.3.2 Virtualization and Containers in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A symphony is moving its donor database from a server it ran itself to a managed database service, a platform as a service (PaaS). Which task MOST clearly stays with the symphony's IT team?

options.A: Setting who may query the database and from which networks
options.B: Patching the database software and the system it runs on
options.C: Replacing failed disks in the provider's storage hardware
options.D: Nothing further, since the provider now runs the database

questions.key_concept: In PaaS the provider maintains the platform software; the customer still controls its data, access rights and service settings.
questions.pre_read: Split the database into the platform that runs it and the data inside it.
questions.correct_explanation: In PaaS, the provider runs and patches the platform, including the database software and the operating system beneath it, while the customer keeps its data, access rights and service settings, such as who may connect and from where. Patching the database software is the runner-up: it was the team's job on its own server, but on PaaS the provider takes it on.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the team did patch the database on its own server. But in PaaS the provider maintains the database software and the system under it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the data lives on those disks. But physical hardware is always the provider's job in a cloud service.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider now runs the platform. But the customer still owns its data, accounts, access rights and settings in every service model.

tips: Eliminate: C is physical hardware, always the provider's, and D forgets that access and settings stay with the customer in every model.
Final two: A beats B because PaaS providers maintain the database software, while who may reach the data stays a customer setting.
Exam cue: in PaaS, the provider runs the platform; the customer secures its code, data, access and settings.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'PaaS offers a managed runtime, database or development platform; the customer secures its own code and settings' (notes 4.3.3 Cloud Service Models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bagel chain spreads its services across three public cloud providers so it does not depend on any one of them. Which security task does this MOST clearly add for the security team?

options.A: Securing the link that moves data between its private and public clouds
options.B: Sharing infrastructure with other firms that follow the same rules
options.C: Buying and running its own data center hardware for the services
options.D: Keeping settings the same in several separate admin consoles

questions.key_concept: Multi-cloud reduces reliance on one provider but adds more consoles and settings to keep consistently secure; hybrid joins different deployment models.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changes when the same work spreads across several providers.
questions.correct_explanation: Using several public providers is multi-cloud: it cuts reliance on any one provider, but each has its own console, settings and defaults, so keeping security settings consistent across them is the added work. Securing a private-to-public link is the runner-up: that is a hybrid cloud's task, where distinct clouds are bound together, and this chain runs no private cloud.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: links between joined clouds do need securing in a hybrid cloud. But this chain uses only public providers, with no private cloud to link.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because several parties are involved. But sharing infrastructure with organizations under common rules describes a community cloud, not one firm using three providers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because spreading out sounds like more infrastructure. But public cloud customers run no data center hardware; that burden comes with a private cloud on their own site.

tips: Eliminate: B describes a community cloud, and C describes running a private cloud on site, while this chain uses public providers.
Final two: D beats A because several public providers multiply the settings to secure, while a private-to-public link belongs to a hybrid cloud.
Exam cue: multi-cloud means several providers and more settings to keep consistent; hybrid means joined deployment models and links to secure.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: deployment models)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Hybrid cloud and multi-cloud mean the same thing' (exam trap, notes 4.3.4 Cloud Deployment Models). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A talent agency's client files leaked after its cloud provider's own staff misconfigured the storage service, and the owner asks who must answer to the clients. Which reply from the system administrator is MOST accurate?

options.A: The provider, because the files were stored on its platform
options.B: The provider, because its own staff made the mistake
options.C: The agency and provider equally, since accountability is shared
options.D: The agency, because accountability for its data stays with it

questions.key_concept: Moving data to the cloud shares duties but not accountability; the customer stays accountable for its data even when the provider errs.
questions.pre_read: Separate who caused the leak from who answers to the clients.
questions.correct_explanation: Contracts can share security duties, but an organization stays accountable for the security and privacy of its data in the cloud, so the agency answers to its clients; it can then seek remedies from the provider under the contract. The provider's mistake is the runner-up: it makes the provider answerable to the agency, not a replacement for the agency's own accountability.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the files sat on the provider's platform. But where data is stored does not move accountability for it away from the organization.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the provider did cause the leak and may owe the agency remedies. But the agency still answers to its own clients for data it chose to put there.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because security duties are shared. But duties can be divided while accountability for the data stays with the organization.

tips: Eliminate: A ties accountability to where data is stored, and C confuses shared duties with shared accountability.
Final two: D beats B because a provider's fault makes it answerable to the agency, while the agency stays accountable to its clients.
Exam cue: duties can be outsourced; accountability for the data stays with the organization that owns it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-144 Section 2.3 (Outsourcing and Accountability)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Moving to the cloud transfers accountability for a data breach to the provider' (exam trap, notes 4.3.5 The Shared Responsibility Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.3 Cloud security. Cloud roles and agreements
questions.question: An estate agency's IT coordinator buys storage, email and backup from one firm that combines three providers' services and negotiates with them on the agency's behalf. Which NIST cloud actor is the firm MOST accurately?

options.A: A cloud provider
options.B: A cloud auditor
options.C: A cloud carrier
options.D: A cloud broker

questions.key_concept: NIST's cloud broker manages and combines cloud services and negotiates between providers and consumers; carriers supply connectivity.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose services the firm is actually selling.
questions.correct_explanation: In NIST's cloud reference architecture, a cloud broker manages the use, performance and delivery of cloud services and negotiates relationships between providers and consumers, often combining several providers' services into one. The provider is the runner-up: a provider makes its own service available, while this firm assembles and manages other providers' services.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the agency does buy its services from this firm. But the firm combines other providers' services and negotiates with them, which NIST calls brokering.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the firm keeps an eye on the services it manages. But a cloud auditor conducts independent assessments of cloud services; it does not sell or manage them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the services reach the agency through the firm. But a cloud carrier provides connectivity and transport, such as network links, not service packages.

tips: Eliminate: B assesses cloud services independently, and C provides the network connectivity that carries cloud services.
Final two: D beats A because the firm combines and manages other providers' services and negotiates with them, rather than offering its own.
Exam cue: combining and negotiating for others is a broker; carrying traffic is a carrier; checking independently is an auditor.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 500-292 Section 2.5 (Cloud Broker: manages the use, performance and delivery of cloud services and negotiates relationships between providers and consumers)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'NIST names the five actors; one organization can play several' (notes 4.3.6 Cloud Roles and Agreements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A ramen chain's data owner labels its AI training data Restricted; procedure has the system administrator encrypt Restricted buckets with the customer-managed key. What should the administrator do FIRST about that data's unencrypted bucket?

options.A: Report the unencrypted bucket to the data owner and await a decision
options.B: Encrypt the bucket with the customer-managed key, and record it
options.C: Delete the bucket's files, as unencrypted data is already exposed
options.D: Encrypt the bucket with the provider-managed key, and record it

questions.key_concept: Protecting the customer's data, AI training data included, is the customer's job in every cloud model, so apply the encryption the procedure assigns.
questions.pre_read: Check what the data owner and the procedure have already decided.
questions.correct_explanation: The data owner has already classified the data, and the procedure gives this exact fix to the administrator, so they encrypt the bucket with the customer-managed key and record the change. Reporting to the data owner is the runner-up: they own the data and its classification, but their decision is already made, and the procedure under it assigns the encryption step.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the data owner does own the training data. But they have already classified it, and the procedure assigns this encryption step to the administrator.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because exposed data feels urgent. But unencrypted is not the same as public, deleting destroys data the business needs, and copies may remain in backups.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a provider-managed key also encrypts the bucket. But the procedure names the customer-managed key, which keeps key control with the chain rather than the provider.

tips: Eliminate: C deletes training data the business needs instead of protecting it, and D uses the provider-managed key, which leaves key control with the provider when the procedure names the customer's key.
Final two: B beats A because the owner's classification and the procedure already decide this step, so the administrator carries it out.
Exam cue: in every cloud model, protecting and keying the customer's own data is the customer's job, so look for the customer-side step the procedure already names.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest); NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.7 (Data Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Classify, encrypt, control the keys and back up: the data is the customer's job in every model' (notes 4.3.7 Protecting Data in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.3 Cloud security. Cloud access security brokers
questions.question: A paint store chain's IT manager says its new cloud access security broker (CASB) just repeats what the network firewall already does. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: A CASB sees which cloud apps staff use and applies data rules
options.B: A CASB filters cloud traffic by IP address and port number
options.C: A CASB blocks web pages by category, such as gambling sites
options.D: A CASB encrypts the traffic between the stores and head office

questions.key_concept: A CASB sits between users and cloud services to reveal app use, shadow IT included, and enforce data rules; web filters only sort sites.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each tool can see that the others cannot.
questions.correct_explanation: A CASB sits between users and cloud services, so it can show which cloud apps staff use, including unapproved ones, and enforce data rules on them, which a firewall filtering by network rules cannot. Category-based web filtering is the runner-up: it also sits in the path, but it sorts sites, not what users do inside cloud apps.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because both sit in the traffic path. But filtering by address and port is a firewall rule, even for cloud traffic; a CASB understands cloud apps, users and data.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: many CASBs do sit in the path like a web proxy. But sorting sites by category shows nothing of what staff do or move inside cloud apps.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both protect traffic. But encrypting links between sites is a VPN's job, not a broker's view into cloud app use.

tips: Eliminate: B describes a network firewall's rules, and D describes a site-to-site VPN; neither understands cloud apps and data.
Final two: A beats C because a CASB understands cloud apps, users and data, while a web filter only sorts sites by category.
Exam cue: a CASB sees inside cloud app use (who, which app, which data); firewalls and web filters see addresses, ports and sites.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-215 Section 3.1 (Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A CASB does the same job as a network firewall' (exam trap, notes 4.3.8 Cloud Misconfiguration, CSPM and CASB). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A sports analytics startup wants to deploy a third-party model from its cloud AI platform's public catalog, which the provider offers as is, without review. Who MOST clearly must vet the model before use?

options.A: The startup, since it chooses which models it deploys
options.B: The provider, since the model sits in its catalog
options.C: The model's uploader, since the startup did not build it
options.D: No one, since popular open models are checked by their users

questions.key_concept: On a cloud AI platform, the provider secures the platform, and the customer must vet the third-party models it chooses to deploy.
questions.pre_read: Ask who decides which model goes into use.
questions.correct_explanation: Shared responsibility for AI follows the service model: the provider secures the platform, while the customer owns the data, models and settings it chooses to use, so a third-party model offered as is must be vetted by the startup, like any outside component. The provider is the runner-up: it hosts the catalog, but it has said plainly that it does not review these models.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the provider does secure the platform and its catalog service. But it offers these third-party models as is, so checking them falls to the customer that deploys them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because authors know their own models. But an unknown uploader owes the startup nothing, and the startup carries the risk of whatever it deploys.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because popular models feel proven. But downloads are not a security review, and tampered or poisoned models can look like ordinary ones.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on an unknown uploader who owes the startup nothing, and D treats popularity as if it were a security review.
Final two: A beats B because the provider offers catalog models as is; the customer owns the models it chooses to run.
Exam cue: on a cloud AI platform, the provider secures the platform, and the customer secures the models and data it brings or picks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 3.2 (Supply Chain Attacks and Mitigations); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 3.1 (AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'An AI service is still a cloud service: the provider secures the platform, and the customer owns its data, models, access and settings' (notes 4.3.9 Shared Responsibility for AI Workloads). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A model railway museum's network technician turns on a switch feature that drops address offers from every device except the approved Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) server. Which risk does this MOST directly reduce?

options.A: A laptop copying another's MAC address to join the network
options.B: An outsider guessing the Wi-Fi passphrase from the car park
options.C: An insider changing the web server's records on the DNS server
options.D: A rogue server sending devices a fake gateway or DNS server

questions.key_concept: DHCP gives each device its address, gateway and DNS settings, so a rogue DHCP server can quietly redirect a device's traffic.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a device accepts from whoever answers its request for network settings.
questions.correct_explanation: DHCP hands each device its IP address plus the gateway and DNS server it should use. A rogue DHCP server can answer first and point devices at an attacker's gateway or DNS, so accepting offers only from the approved server blocks that. Copying a MAC address is the runner-up: it is also a local network trick, but other controls, such as network access control (NAC), deal with it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: MAC copying is also a local network trick. But port security or network access control (NAC) handles it, not filtering DHCP offers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because outsiders do attack Wi-Fi. But a guessed passphrase is a wireless encryption problem, and filtering DHCP offers on switches does nothing about it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a rogue DHCP server can also point devices at a fake DNS server. But editing records on the real DNS server needs access control there.

tips: Eliminate: B is a wireless passphrase problem, and C is about who can edit records on the real DNS server; filtering DHCP offers touches neither.
Final two: D beats A because the feature blocks unapproved DHCP answers, which is how a rogue server feeds devices a fake gateway or DNS; MAC copying needs NAC or port security.
Exam cue: DHCP and DNS are trusted plumbing; a control that limits who may answer them protects every device that asks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-119 Section 4.7.3 (Security Ramifications: rogue responses from unauthorized DHCP servers can distribute false information and misroute packets); NIST SP 800-81 Rev. 3 Section 1.1 (Domain Name Systems: translating domain names into IP addresses is called name resolution)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) hands out IP addresses; the Domain Name System (DNS) turns names into IP addresses' (notes 4.1.1 Network Building Blocks). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A fabric store's card reader has a link light and pings devices on its subnet, but not the payment server on another. Which Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) layer should the IT technician check FIRST?

options.A: Layer 1, the physical layer
options.B: Layer 2, the data link layer
options.C: Layer 3, the network layer
options.D: Layer 4, the transport layer

questions.key_concept: Troubleshoot by layer: what already works rules out the layers below it, and reaching another subnet depends on IP routing at layer 3.
questions.pre_read: List what already works, then find the first job that fails.
questions.correct_explanation: The link light shows layer 1 works, and pinging devices on its own subnet shows frames are delivered locally, so layers 1 and 2 are fine. Reaching another subnet needs routing by IP address, which is layer 3, so the gateway and routes come next. The transport layer is the runner-up, but ping uses ICMP, which has no port numbers, so port rules cannot explain a failed ping.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because cabling faults are common. But the link light is on and local pings succeed, so the physical connection works.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because switches deliver local traffic. But local pings succeed, so frames reach neighbors; the failure starts where traffic must leave the subnet.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: firewall port rules often block traffic. But ping uses ICMP, a network layer protocol with no ports, so a transport-layer port rule cannot explain this.

tips: Eliminate: A falls because the link light and local pings prove the cable works, and B because local pings prove frames reach neighbors.
Final two: C beats D because leaving the subnet depends on IP routing at layer 3, and ping uses ICMP, which has no ports to block at layer 4.
Exam cue: work up the layers: what already works rules out the layers below it, and the first thing that fails names the layer to check.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2 (Overview of Firewall Technologies: the network layer routes packets across networks, and ICMP is a network layer protocol); NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Appendix B Glossary (router)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Name the layer before the fix' (notes 4.1.2 The OSI Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A canal boat hire firm's office volunteer says its new plain switch works at layer 3 because it connects all the office computers. Which reply from the network technician is MOST accurate?

options.A: It works at layer 3, since it reads packets' IP addresses
options.B: It works at layer 1, since it repeats signals to every port
options.C: It works at layer 4, since its sockets are numbered ports
options.D: It works at layer 2, since it forwards frames by MAC address

questions.key_concept: A plain switch forwards frames by MAC address inside one network, at layer 2; routing by IP address between networks is layer 3.
questions.pre_read: Ask which address the device reads to decide where data goes.
questions.correct_explanation: A plain switch forwards frames inside one local network by their MAC address, which is layer 2, the data link layer. Reading IP addresses to move packets between networks is a router's layer 3 job; only a layer 3 switch adds routing. That is the runner-up: connecting many computers does not make a device a router.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: layer 3 switches do exist and route by IP address. But a plain switch only forwards frames by MAC address inside one network.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because older hubs did this. But repeating every signal out of every port is a layer 1 hub's behavior, not a switch's.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a switch's sockets are called ports. But those are physical connectors; transport-layer port numbers name services inside the traffic.

tips: Eliminate: B describes a hub, which repeats every signal at layer 1, and C confuses a switch's physical sockets with transport-layer port numbers.
Final two: D beats A because a plain switch forwards frames by MAC address inside one network; reading IP addresses to route between networks is layer 3 work.
Exam cue: name a device's layer by the address it reads: MAC means layer 2, IP means layer 3, port numbers mean layer 4.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2 (Overview of Firewall Technologies: data link layer addresses assigned to network interfaces are MAC addresses); NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Appendix B Glossary (router)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A switch is a layer 3 device because it connects computers' (exam trap, notes 4.1.2 The OSI Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A salt mine's log server collects device logs over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), and during busy hours some entries never arrive. What should the system administrator conclude MOST likely explains the gaps?

options.A: TCP drops log entries that arrive out of order on busy links
options.B: UDP encrypts each entry, and some fail to decrypt in time
options.C: A three-way handshake times out when the server is busy
options.D: UDP sends each entry once, with no delivery check or resend

questions.key_concept: UDP sends each datagram once with no acknowledgment or resend, so lost data is simply gone; TCP confirms delivery.
questions.pre_read: Recall which transport protocol checks that data arrived and which does not.
questions.correct_explanation: UDP sends each datagram once, with no handshake, acknowledgment or resend, so when links or the server are busy, lost log entries are simply gone. NIST's log management guide notes this weakness of syslog over UDP and points to TCP for reliable delivery. The handshake answer is the runner-up, but the three-way handshake belongs to TCP; UDP never sets up a connection.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because TCP features appear in many log tools. But these logs travel over UDP, and TCP reorders and resends data rather than dropping it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because secure logging matters. But UDP itself encrypts nothing; encryption comes from a protocol on top, such as TLS.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: busy servers do time out connections. But the three-way handshake belongs to TCP; UDP sends without setting up any connection to time out.

tips: Eliminate: A blames TCP, which these logs do not use and which resends lost data, and B gives UDP encryption, which it does not provide.
Final two: D beats C because UDP has no handshake to time out; it simply sends each datagram once and never knows whether it arrived.
Exam cue: missing pieces with no error point to UDP; when every piece must arrive, choose TCP, which acknowledges and resends.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-92 Section 3.3.2 (Syslog Security: UDP provides no assurance that log entries are received successfully or in the correct sequence); NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.2 (Stateful Inspection: tracking TCP connection state)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The User Datagram Protocol (UDP) sends each datagram alone, with no delivery check' (notes 4.1.3 The TCP/IP Model, TCP and UDP). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A costume rental shop's network technician reviews a firewall rule allowing the source 192.168.10.0/24 to reach the payroll server. Which addresses does the rule MOST accurately allow?

options.B: Only the single device at 192.168.10.24
options.D: Any address ending in .24 on any 192.168 subnet

questions.key_concept: In CIDR notation, the number after the slash counts the network bits; a /24 fixes the first three numbers of an IPv4 address.
questions.pre_read: Work out how many of the address's four numbers the slash value fixes.
questions.correct_explanation: In Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) notation, the number after the slash counts the leading bits that name the network. A /24 fixes the first 24 bits, the first three numbers, so the rule covers 192.168.10.0 to 192.168.10.255. The 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255 range is the runner-up, but that is a /16, which fixes only the first two numbers and allows far more devices.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because 24 appears in the rule. But /24 counts network bits, not a host number; a single device would be written /32.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: this is a real private range. But it is 192.168.0.0/16; a /24 fixes three numbers, so only the 192.168.10 addresses match.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the 24 looks like the last number. But the slash value counts leading bits; it never matches addresses by their ending.

tips: Eliminate: B and D both read the 24 as part of an address, but after the slash it counts the leading bits that name the network.
Final two: A beats C because /24 fixes the first three numbers, 192.168.10; the wider 192.168.0.0 range needs /16.
Exam cue: in CIDR, a bigger number after the slash means a smaller range; /32 is one address, and each step down doubles it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-119 Section 3.1.6 (IPv4 Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) Addressing: the number after the slash gives how many leading bits form the network address); NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 4.1.1 (IP Addresses and Other IP Characteristics: 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255 is 192.168.0.0/16 in CIDR notation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) notation, as in 10.0.0.0/8, shows how many leading bits name the network' (notes 4.1.4 IPv4 and IPv6). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A glove maker's public web server offers Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) 3.0 and Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.0, 1.2 and 1.3, and its owner asks the system administrator which to keep. Which advice is BEST?

options.A: Only TLS 1.3, since every earlier version is retired
options.B: All four, so every visitor's browser can still connect
options.C: All four, with the oldest two moved to an unusual port
options.D: TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3, switching every older version off

questions.key_concept: Servers should offer TLS 1.2 and 1.3 and turn off SSL and early TLS; TLS 1.2 is still current, not retired.
questions.pre_read: Sort the four versions into current and retired before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST's TLS guide says public servers must support TLS 1.2 and, since 2024, TLS 1.3, must not allow SSL 3.0, and discourages TLS 1.0; it allows switching 1.2 off only where it is confirmed unneeded. So this server keeps 1.2 and 1.3 and turns the older versions off. TLS 1.3 alone is the runner-up: it is the strongest version, but TLS 1.2 is still current, and many visitors' browsers and devices still rely on it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: TLS 1.3 is the strongest version. But TLS 1.2 is not retired; it is still approved, and many visitors' devices need it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because compatibility matters. But keeping SSL 3.0 and TLS 1.0 lets attackers push connections down to weak versions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fewer scans sounds safer. But scanners find services on any port, and the old versions stay just as weak.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps SSL 3.0 and TLS 1.0, which attackers can force connections down to, and C moves old versions to another port, where scanners still find them and they stay weak.
Final two: D beats A because TLS 1.2 is still current and approved; only SSL and early TLS should go, so 1.2 and 1.3 both stay.
Exam cue: for TLS, keep 1.2 and 1.3 and switch off everything older; 'newest only' is not the rule.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 Section 3.1 (Protocol Version Support: servers shall support TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 and shall not allow SSL 2.0 or SSL 3.0); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-7 (Least Functionality)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Transport Layer Security (TLS): use version 1.2 or 1.3, never the retired Secure Sockets Layer (SSL)' (notes 4.1.5 Ports, Protocols and Secure Alternatives). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A weather service's network technician is making a training slide that pairs cleartext protocols with their secure replacements. Which pairing is MOST accurate?

options.A: SNMP version 1 replaced by SNMP version 2c for monitoring
options.B: HTTP replaced by SFTP for secure web page browsing
options.C: Telnet replaced by SSH for remote command logins
options.D: FTP replaced by FTP on an unusual high port number

questions.key_concept: A secure replacement does the same job with encryption: SSH for Telnet, SFTP for FTP, HTTPS for HTTP and SNMP version 3 for earlier versions.
questions.pre_read: For each pair, ask whether the second protocol does the same job and encrypts it.
questions.correct_explanation: Telnet sends logins and commands in cleartext; Secure Shell (SSH) does the same remote command-line job inside an encrypted channel, so it is the standard replacement. SNMP version 2c is the runner-up because it is newer than version 1, but it still sends its community strings in cleartext; version 3 is the version that adds encryption.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: version 2c is newer than version 1. But it still sends its community strings in cleartext; only SNMP version 3 adds encryption.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because SFTP is a secure protocol. But SFTP moves files over SSH; secure web browsing uses HTTPS, which wraps HTTP in TLS.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because unusual ports draw fewer scans. But changing the port encrypts nothing; FTP is replaced by SFTP or FTPS.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps a web protocol for a file-transfer one, and D only moves FTP to another port, which encrypts nothing.
Final two: C beats A because SSH encrypts the same remote login job Telnet does in cleartext, while SNMP version 2c still sends its community strings unencrypted.
Exam cue: a secure replacement does the same job with encryption: SSH for Telnet, SFTP for FTP, HTTPS for HTTP, SNMP version 3 for earlier versions.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 6.2.10 (Remote Access: SSH is a secure alternative to a telnet application); NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Table 19 (Communication and network configuration vulnerabilities: protocols such as telnet, FTP and HTTP send data in plaintext)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Choose the encrypted protocol for the same job: SSH over Telnet, SFTP over FTP, HTTPS over HTTP' (notes 4.1.5 Ports, Protocols and Secure Alternatives). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A dance company will link its rehearsal studio's network to head office so devices reach servers at the other site, with no software on each device. Which setup should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: A TLS VPN app installed on each studio computer
options.B: An IPsec site-to-site tunnel between the two gateways
options.C: Port forwarding that opens head office servers to the internet
options.D: HTTPS on each server, with no tunnel between the sites

questions.key_concept: An IPsec site-to-site (gateway-to-gateway) VPN protects all traffic between two networks with no software on each device; client VPNs suit individual remote users.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether two whole networks or individual people need connecting.
questions.correct_explanation: An IPsec site-to-site VPN joins the two networks at their gateways and encrypts all traffic between the sites at the network layer, so studio devices need no software. A TLS VPN app is the runner-up: it suits remote users, but it means installing and managing a client on every device, which the company wants to avoid.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: TLS VPNs are common and secure. But they suit individual remote users and need a client on each device, which the company wants to avoid.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is quick to set up. But it exposes internal servers to everyone on the internet, often without encryption.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because HTTPS encrypts. But it protects only web traffic to each server; other traffic between the sites would cross the internet unprotected.

tips: Eliminate: C exposes internal servers to the whole internet, and D protects only web traffic, leaving the rest of the site-to-site traffic unprotected.
Final two: B beats A because a site-to-site IPsec tunnel protects all traffic between the two networks at their gateways, with no software on each device.
Exam cue: joining two networks points to an IPsec site-to-site VPN; one remote person on a laptop points to a client or TLS VPN.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1 Section 2.4.1 (Gateway-to-Gateway: a VPN gateway on each network protects the traffic between the two networks); NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1 Section 2.3 (Virtual Private Networking (VPN))
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IP Security (IPsec) works at the network layer and suits site-to-site links; Transport Layer Security (TLS) VPNs suit remote users' (notes 4.1.6 Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A spice shop's card terminals stopped taking payments at 14:05, just after a new firewall rule went live at 14:00. Which evidence should the network technician check FIRST to confirm the rule is the cause?

options.A: Firewall log entries that deny payment traffic after 14:00
options.B: The payment provider's status page for any reported outage
options.C: The firewall's logged processor and memory use since 14:00
options.D: A packet capture taken on a laptop in the shop's back office

questions.key_concept: When a failure follows a change, confirm the cause from the trace that change would leave, such as firewall entries denying the traffic.
questions.pre_read: Think about where the payment traffic passes and what each source can show about it.
questions.correct_explanation: A rule that blocks traffic leaves a trace: the firewall logs each connection it denies. Deny entries for payment traffic starting at 14:00 tie the outage to the new rule, so the fix can go through change management with evidence behind it. The provider's status page is the runner-up: it can rule out an outage on the provider's side, but a clear page does not show the rule is to blame.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: checking the provider rules out one other cause. But a quiet status page proves nothing about the new rule; only the firewall's own records show it blocking payments.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an overloaded firewall can drop traffic. But load figures cannot show a rule denying payments, and one new rule rarely changes them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because captures show real traffic. But on a switched network a back-office laptop normally sees only its own traffic, and a capture cannot show which rule dropped anything.

tips: Eliminate: C looks at firewall load, which cannot show a rule denying traffic, and D captures on a back-office laptop, which on a switched network does not normally see the card terminals' traffic.
Final two: A beats B because deny entries for payment traffic from 14:00 tie the outage to the new rule; a clear status page only rules out the provider.
Exam cue: when a failure follows a change, look for the trace the change would leave before deciding the cause.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Allow only what the business needs with the narrowest rule, deny the rest, and change rules only through change management' (notes 4.1.7 Firewalls: Ports and Applications). Re-angled in fix-up round 2 because the emergency-rollback lesson repeated cc_d5_107. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A coffee roaster wants a firewall that ends each staff web connection and opens its own to the site, inspecting the content between. Which firewall type should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: A stateful inspection firewall that tracks each connection
options.B: A packet-filtering router that checks each packet's addresses and ports
options.C: A network address translation device that swaps addresses
options.D: A proxy firewall that relays each connection through itself

questions.key_concept: A proxy firewall ends the client's connection and opens its own to the server; a stateful firewall tracks connections it lets pass.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the device lets the original connection pass or replaces it with its own.
questions.correct_explanation: A proxy firewall, which NIST calls an application-proxy gateway, never lets the two hosts connect directly: it holds one connection with the client and opens a second to the server, inspecting the content between them. A stateful firewall is the runner-up: it tracks each connection's state, but it passes the original connection through rather than ending and relaying it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: stateful firewalls do track every connection. But they let the original connection pass through; they do not end it and open their own.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is a common first filter. But it judges each packet by address and port alone, without ending connections or reading content.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it sits in the path and rewrites traffic. But address translation only changes addresses; it neither inspects content nor relays connections.

tips: Eliminate: B judges packets only by address and port, and C only rewrites addresses; neither ends connections or reads content.
Final two: D beats A because a proxy firewall ends the client's connection and opens its own to the server, while a stateful firewall passes the original connection through.
Exam cue: 'two separate connections with inspection between' means a proxy; 'tracks connection state' means stateful; 'address and port only' means a packet filter.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.4 (Application-Proxy Gateways: the proxy creates two separate connections and never allows a direct connection between the hosts); NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.2 (Stateful Inspection: tracking TCP connection state)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Proxy firewall: ends the client's connection and opens a new one to the server, inspecting the traffic between' (notes 4.1.7 Firewalls: Ports and Applications). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A watch parts wholesaler's inline intrusion prevention system (IPS) guards its order servers; the system owner decided orders must keep flowing if it crashes. Which setup should the network technician choose as BEST?

options.A: Fail closed, blocking all traffic until the IPS is back up
options.B: Put the IPS on a mirror port, where crashes cannot stop orders
options.C: Fail open, passing traffic uninspected until the IPS is back up
options.D: Set the IPS to alert-only, so it logs attacks without blocking

questions.key_concept: An inline IPS must fail one way: open keeps traffic flowing uninspected, closed keeps protection but stops traffic; the owner's risk decision picks which.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens to traffic passing through an inline device when that device stops working.
questions.correct_explanation: An inline IPS sits in the traffic path, so its failure setting decides what happens when it crashes. Fail open lets traffic pass uninspected until it recovers, which matches the owner's decision that orders must keep flowing. Fail closed is the runner-up: it keeps protection, but it stops every order, the outcome the owner ruled out.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: failing closed keeps unchecked traffic out. But it stops every order during a crash, and the system owner has decided orders must keep flowing.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a mirror-port sensor cannot stop traffic. But it can no longer block attacks either, which gives up prevention all the time to cover rare crashes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because alert-only mode never blocks business traffic. But it also never blocks attacks, so the IPS stops preventing anything, not just during a crash.

tips: Eliminate: B and D both give up blocking for good; a mirror-port sensor or alert-only mode cannot stop any attack, though the owner decided only what happens during a crash.
Final two: C beats A because the owner chose to keep orders flowing if the IPS fails; failing closed protects more but stops the orders the owner said must continue.
Exam cue: an inline device fails one of two ways: open keeps the business running unprotected, closed keeps protection and stops the business; the owner's risk decision picks which.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-24 (Fail in Known State); NIST SP 800-94 Section 4.2.2 (Network Architectures and Sensor Locations: inline versus passive sensors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Traffic may stop, unless it fails open' (notes 4.1.8 Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. AI in traffic monitoring
questions.question: A surf school's IT manager says a planned artificial intelligence (AI) traffic monitor is pointless, because nearly all its traffic is encrypted. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Encrypted traffic leaves the model nothing it can analyze
options.B: It decrypts each session by itself to read the hidden content
options.C: Timing, volume and destinations still show unusual patterns
options.D: Only fixed signature rules can judge encrypted sessions

questions.key_concept: Encryption hides content, not patterns: AI monitors still learn timing, volume and destinations, and flag unusual behavior in encrypted traffic.
questions.pre_read: Separate what encryption hides from what it leaves visible.
questions.correct_explanation: Encryption hides what is inside a session, not its pattern. An AI monitor can still learn who talks to whom, when and how much, and flag a laptop suddenly sending large volumes at night to a new destination. The decryption answer is the runner-up: some separate tools inspect encrypted traffic with special setup, but a traffic monitor cannot read encrypted content on its own.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the content is hidden. But timing, volume and destinations stay visible, and they are what the model scores against its baseline.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: some inspection setups do decrypt traffic. But that needs keys or a proxy; on its own, the monitor works from patterns, not content.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because signatures are familiar. But signatures need readable content to match; encrypted traffic is where pattern-based AI adds the most.

tips: Eliminate: A forgets that traffic patterns stay visible, and D credits signatures, which need readable content, with seeing inside encryption.
Final two: C beats B because the monitor learns patterns from what stays visible; reading content needs keys or a separate inspection setup it does not have.
Exam cue: encryption hides the message, not the envelope: timing, size and destination still tell a story.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-94 Section 2.3.2 (Anomaly-Based Detection); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-4(13) (System Monitoring | Analyze Traffic and Event Patterns)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI monitoring sees nothing in encrypted traffic' (exam trap, notes 4.1.9 AI in Traffic Monitoring, IDS and Firewalls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. AI in traffic monitoring
questions.question: A cable TV company's vendor says its artificial intelligence (AI) firewall would let the company drop night-shift analysts, since the AI blocks attacks itself. Which reply from the security manager is MOST accurate?

options.A: It will still miss some attacks and flag some safe traffic
options.B: After a month of learning normal traffic, the cut is likely safe
options.C: It blocks known attacks well, so one analyst on call is enough
options.D: AI firewalls only alert, so analysts do all the blocking

questions.key_concept: AI detection is a strong assistant, not a final judge: it still makes false positives and false negatives, and attackers try to evade it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the vendor's claim assumes about how the AI will behave once it is running.
questions.correct_explanation: Machine learning still produces false positives and false negatives, and attackers deliberately try to evade it, so AI detection is a strong assistant, not a final judge. People must review its alerts and decide high-impact actions. A month of baseline is the runner-up: learning normal traffic helps accuracy, but no baseline removes misses, false alarms or evasion.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a good baseline does improve accuracy. But no amount of learning removes false alarms, misses or attackers' attempts to evade the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it keeps a person in the loop. But one on-call analyst cannot review the misses and false alarms an AI firewall still produces overnight.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because classic IDS tools only alert. But AI firewalls can block; the point is that their blocks and alerts still need human review.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves one on-call analyst to catch what the AI misses or wrongly flags, and D wrongly says AI firewalls cannot block traffic.
Final two: A beats B because a longer baseline improves accuracy but never removes misses, false alarms or evasion, so people stay in the loop.
Exam cue: AI in security operations assists analysts; any option that removes human review of its output is the trap.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 2.2 (Evasion Attacks and Mitigations: adversarial examples change a model's output with only minimal changes to the input); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 3.2 (roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems are defined)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'An AI-powered firewall removes the need for analysts' (exam trap, notes 4.1.9 AI in Traffic Monitoring, IDS and Firewalls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Blind re-test fix (5 Nov 2026): C given a measured but still wrong claim, so the key is not the only cautious option.

questions.question: A roller rink's owner wants to keep its old access point on Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP), using the longest key it allows, to save money. Which reply from the IT technician is MOST accurate?

options.A: A full 128-bit WEP key is strong enough for a small business
options.B: Changing the WEP key every month will keep attackers out
options.C: Switching to the first WPA on the same device is enough
options.D: WEP is broken at any key length; upgrade to WPA3 or WPA2

questions.key_concept: WEP is broken by design, whatever its key length; use WPA3, or WPA2 where devices cannot do WPA3.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the weakness lies in the key's size or in the protocol itself.
questions.correct_explanation: WEP's design is broken, so attackers can recover its key with free tools whatever the key length; NIST notes it was deprecated in 2004. The access point should move to WPA3, or WPA2 where devices cannot do WPA3. A long 128-bit key is the runner-up because longer keys usually mean stronger encryption, but WEP's flaw is in how it uses the key, not its size.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: longer keys usually do mean stronger encryption. But WEP's weakness is in its design, so even its longest key is quickly broken.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because changing keys often limits exposure. But free tools recover a WEP key from captured traffic in minutes, long before any monthly change.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because WPA was built to replace WEP. But the first WPA was a stopgap built on WEP's cipher and is retired too; use WPA3, or WPA2.

tips: Eliminate: B changes a key that free tools recover in minutes, and C moves to the first WPA, a stopgap on WEP's cipher that is retired too.
Final two: D beats A because WEP is broken by design; a longer key does not fix how it uses the key, so it must be replaced.
Exam cue: for Wi-Fi, pick the strongest standard the devices support, WPA3 first; never WEP or the first WPA, whatever the key.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1 Section 8.1.1 (WiFi Data Link Protection); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-18(1) (Wireless Access | Authentication and Encryption)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) and the first Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) are broken; use WPA3, or WPA2 where devices cannot do WPA3' (notes 4.1.10 Wireless Security: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. Embedded and control systems
questions.question: A road tunnel operator's IT manager says the ventilation control network needs no malware defenses, because it has no link to the internet. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Malware cannot reach a network that has no internet link
options.B: USB drives and vendor laptops still bring in malware by hand
options.C: It needs only a yearly check that no internet link exists
options.D: It needs weekly patching, the same as the office laptops

questions.key_concept: An air gap narrows the ways in but does not close them: removable media, vendor laptops and forgotten links have carried malware into control networks.
questions.pre_read: Test each reply against how isolated control networks have actually been attacked.
questions.correct_explanation: Isolation removes the internet path, but people still carry files and devices in: USB drives, vendor maintenance laptops and forgotten links have all brought malware into isolated control networks. NIST's operational technology guide says air gaps alone are not enough and that portable devices should be scanned before they connect. A yearly link check is the runner-up: it keeps the gap honest, but it ignores the drives and laptops that cross it by hand.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the internet is the usual route in. But malware has reached isolated plants on USB drives and vendor laptops, with no internet link at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: checking that the gap still holds is useful. But it covers only internet links, not the drives and laptops people carry across it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because patching protects office laptops. But control system patches are tested and scheduled first, since an untested patch can stop the fans.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes no internet link means no way in, and D puts control systems on the office laptops' patch schedule, which risks stopping the fans.
Final two: B beats C because a yearly link check keeps the gap intact but misses the USB drives and vendor laptops that people carry across it.
Exam cue: an air gap is a strong control, not a guarantee; ask what people carry across it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 3.2 (Business Case for the OT Cybersecurity Program: relying on traditional measures such as air gaps is not enough); NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 6.2.1.2 (Physical Access Controls: scan portable devices such as laptops and USB storage before they connect to OT networks)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'An ICS network with no internet link cannot be attacked' (exam trap, notes 4.1.11 Embedded Systems and Industrial Control Systems). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An intruder who took over a receptionist's computer at a soap maker then signs in to the file server and the backup server. Which placement would BEST have kept the backup server out of reach?

options.A: In the server segment, next to the file server it backs up
options.B: In the screened subnet (DMZ), apart from the internal network
options.C: On its own VLAN, with routing open to all other segments
options.D: In its own segment, open to backup traffic and nothing else

questions.key_concept: Keep backups out of reach of the systems they protect: give the backup server its own segment that accepts only backup traffic.
questions.pre_read: Trace the intruder's path, then ask what each placement would leave within reach.
questions.correct_explanation: A backup exists for the day the systems it copies are compromised, so it must not fall with them. Its own segment, with rules that accept backup traffic and block everything else, keeps sign-ins from desk computers, or from a taken-over file server, away from it. Placing it beside the file server is the runner-up: grouping servers apart from desks is sound, but a shared segment lets whoever reaches one server reach the other.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: grouping servers apart from desk computers is sound. But the intruder reached the file server too, and a shared segment would let them reach the backups from there.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a screened subnet sits apart from the internal network. But it holds public-facing servers, so it would expose the backups more, not less.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because its own VLAN sounds separate. But with routing open to every segment, the intruder could still reach it; only rules on the traffic between segments protect it.

tips: Eliminate: B puts the backups in the screened subnet meant for public-facing servers, and C gives them a VLAN whose open routing lets every segment reach it.
Final two: D beats A because the intruder also reached the file server; backups sharing its segment would be reachable from there, while a segment open only to backup traffic keeps sign-ins out.
Exam cue: keep a backup out of reach of the systems it protects; a segment that accepts only the traffic it needs stops one breach from reaching both.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7(21) (Boundary Protection | Isolation of System Components); NIST SP 800-215 Section 2.1 (Limitations of Network Perimeter-based Protections: east-west traffic stays within the local network)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Lateral movement: an attacker moving from a first compromised system to other systems inside the network' (notes 4.2.1 Network Segmentation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Re-angled in the batch 6 fix round from an attack-terms quiz (5.2 content) to a segmentation decision; the intrusion is context only. Avoids the lessons of cc_d4_010, cc_d4_026 and cc_d4_052.

questions.question: A comedy club's booking server holds members' card details and must stay on the internal network, yet the public needs its booking pages. Which setup should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Move the booking server into the screened subnet
options.B: Forward a public port straight to the booking server
options.C: Put a reverse proxy in the screened subnet to relay requests
options.D: Open the inner firewall to all web traffic from the internet

questions.key_concept: When a system holding sensitive data must stay internal, a relay such as a reverse proxy in the screened subnet faces the public for it.
questions.pre_read: Place each part by who must reach it and what data it holds.
questions.correct_explanation: A reverse proxy in the screened subnet takes the public's requests and relays only valid ones to the internal booking server, so the internet never connects to it directly and the card data stays deeper inside. Moving the server into the screened subnet is the runner-up: public-facing servers do belong there, but this one holds card details, which must stay internal.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: public-facing servers usually belong in the screened subnet. But this server holds card details, which must stay on the internal network.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is quick. But it lets anyone on the internet connect straight to the internal server, which the design must avoid.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because only web traffic is opened. But it lets the whole internet reach every internal web service, not just the booking pages.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the internet connect straight to the internal server, and D opens every internal web service to the whole internet.
Final two: C beats A because the server holding card details stays internal, while a reverse proxy in the screened subnet faces the public for it.
Exam cue: place each system by who must reach it; when sensitive data must stay inside, put a relay in the screened subnet instead.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 3.1 (Network Layouts with Firewalls: public-facing servers on the DMZ); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7 (Boundary Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Reverse proxy: a server that receives public requests and passes them to internal servers, hiding those servers' (notes 4.2.2 Firewall Zones and the Screened Subnet (DMZ)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A science museum's network technician must carry the staff, guest and camera virtual local area networks (VLANs) over the one cable joining two switches. Which setup is BEST?

options.A: An access port set to the staff VLAN on each switch
options.B: A hub between the switches that repeats all frames
options.C: A trunk link that tags each frame with its VLAN number
options.D: Port mirroring that copies traffic between the switches

questions.key_concept: A trunk link carries several VLANs over one cable by tagging each frame (802.1Q); an access port carries a single VLAN.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the receiving switch can tell which VLAN each frame belongs to.
questions.correct_explanation: A trunk link carries several VLANs over one cable by tagging each frame with its VLAN number, the 802.1Q standard, so the receiving switch keeps each VLAN's traffic separate. An access port is the runner-up: it is the normal setting for a device's port, but it belongs to one VLAN, so the guest and camera traffic could not cross.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: access ports are the usual setting for device ports. But each belongs to one VLAN, so the guest and camera traffic could not cross.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a hub joins cables simply. But it works at layer 1, knows nothing of VLANs and repeats every frame to every port.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it also sends traffic between ports. But mirroring copies traffic to a monitoring tool; it does not carry VLANs between switches.

tips: Eliminate: B uses a layer 1 hub, which knows nothing of VLANs, and D mirrors copies of traffic for monitoring rather than carrying it.
Final two: C beats A because a trunk tags each frame with its VLAN so several VLANs share one cable; an access port carries only one.
Exam cue: one VLAN per device port is an access port; several VLANs between switches means a tagged trunk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Appendix E.1.3 (Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs): switches logically separate traffic based on switch ports); NIST SP 800-119 Section 6.4.1 (Deployment of a Dual Stack Environment: 802.1q tags can be used to divide a network logically)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Each switch port belongs to a VLAN; trunk links between switches carry several VLANs, tagging each frame (the 802.1Q standard)' (notes 4.2.3 Virtual LANs (VLANs)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A lens maker's network technician says micro-segmentation is just splitting the data center into many tiny virtual local area networks (VLANs). Which reply from the system administrator is MOST accurate?

options.A: It applies policy to each workload, even two on the same VLAN
options.B: It puts each server in its own VLAN, behind a router
options.C: It replaces the edge firewall with rules on each server
options.D: It needs a hardware firewall in front of every server

questions.key_concept: Micro-segmentation applies policy to each workload, often by label, and can separate two machines on the same VLAN; VLANs group switch ports.
questions.pre_read: Compare what a VLAN groups with what micro-segmentation protects.
questions.correct_explanation: Micro-segmentation applies policy to each workload, such as a server, virtual machine or container, often by its label rather than its address, so it can keep apart even two machines on the same VLAN. Giving each server its own VLAN is the runner-up: it shrinks segments, but VLANs group switch ports and still need filtering between them.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: tiny VLANs do shrink segments. But VLANs group switch ports, while micro-segmentation sets rules on each workload, even inside one VLAN.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rules move onto each server. But micro-segmentation adds to the edge firewall; defense in depth keeps both.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because firewalls enforce the rules. But micro-segmentation is usually enforced in host firewalls, the virtualization platform or cloud security groups, not by a separate box per server.

tips: Eliminate: C treats micro-segmentation as a replacement for the edge firewall, and D thinks it needs a hardware box per server, when host firewalls or the platform enforce it.
Final two: A beats B because micro-segmentation sets policy on each workload, even inside one VLAN, while VLANs group switch ports.
Exam cue: VLANs divide switch ports; micro-segmentation wraps each workload in its own rules, which follow it wherever it runs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-215 Section 5.1 (Microsegmentation); NIST SP 800-207 Section 3.1.2 (ZTA Using Micro-Segmentation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Micro-segmentation is simply smaller VLANs' (exam trap, notes 4.2.4 Micro-Segmentation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Defense in depth
questions.question: A map publisher protects its artificial intelligence (AI) training data with an edge firewall, a separate network segment and multifactor sign-in. Which addition should the security analyst propose as BEST for defense in depth?

options.A: Give the training data its own segment, behind a second firewall
options.B: Replace the edge firewall with a newer, stronger model
options.C: Make staff change passwords monthly, and log each change
options.D: Encrypt the stored training data, and log each read of it

questions.key_concept: Defense in depth runs from the outside in to the data itself; when every layer guards the path, add protection on the data.
questions.pre_read: Sort the existing controls by where they sit, from the edge inward.
questions.correct_explanation: All three current controls guard the paths to the data: the edge, the segment and the sign-in. Defense in depth reaches the data itself, so the next layer belongs there. Encryption keeps stored copies, disks and backups unreadable without the key, and logging each read shows who touched the data, even an account that got past every path. A second firewall is the runner-up: it helps, but it is one more path layer.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a tighter segment does make the path harder. But it is another layer on the path, and nothing yet protects the data itself once a path is breached.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because newer firewalls catch more. But replacing a layer adds no new one; the edge stays a single layer, just upgraded.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because passwords guard sign-in. But forced monthly changes push people toward weaker, predictable passwords, and multifactor sign-in already covers that layer.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps one edge firewall for another, which adds no layer, and C forces monthly password changes, which weaken passwords on a layer multifactor already covers.
Final two: D beats A because every current control guards the path to the data; a second firewall is one more path layer, while encryption and read logging protect the data itself.
Exam cue: map the layers from the outside in; if every control guards the way to the data, add one on the data itself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-8(1) (Security and Privacy Architectures | Defense in Depth); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Layers run from the outside in, from physical security to the data itself, as the diagram shows' (notes 4.2.5 Defense in Depth). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust principles
questions.question: At a clock museum adopting Zero Trust, the security team designs logging and access rules as if an attacker were already inside the network. Which principle does this MOST directly apply?

options.A: Assume breach
options.B: Trust but verify
options.C: Implicit trust
options.D: Security by obscurity

questions.key_concept: Assume breach means designing defenses as if an attacker is already inside, so access stays narrow and damage is found and limited quickly.
questions.pre_read: Match the team's starting assumption to the principle that names it.
questions.correct_explanation: Assume breach means designing defenses as if an attacker is already inside, so access stays narrow, activity is logged, and damage is found and limited quickly. NIST's Zero Trust guide says assets should act as if an attacker is present on the enterprise network. Trust but verify is the runner-up: it sounds similar, but it starts from trust, which Zero Trust never grants for location alone.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it does include verifying. But it starts by trusting; Zero Trust starts from no trust and assumes an attacker may already be inside.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it sounds like a design choice. But implicit trust means trusting anything inside a zone without checks, which Zero Trust works to remove.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because hiding things can slow attackers. But obscurity relies on secrecy, while this design relies on logging and narrow access.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts everything inside a zone, the opposite of Zero Trust, and D relies on hiding things rather than on logging and narrow access.
Final two: A beats B because designing as if an attacker is already inside is assume breach; trust but verify still begins by trusting.
Exam cue: Zero Trust in three phrases: verify explicitly, grant least privilege, assume breach.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 2.2 (A Zero Trust View of a Network: assets should always act as if an attacker is present on the enterprise network); NIST SP 800-207 Section 2.1 (Tenets of Zero Trust)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Verify explicitly, grant least privilege, assume breach' (notes 4.2.6 Zero Trust Principles). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust components
questions.question: At a shipping insurer, the Zero Trust policy engine approves an artificial intelligence (AI) agent's request. Which component does the security analyst MOST accurately expect to tell the enforcement point to open the session?

options.A: The policy engine, which made the decision
options.B: The AI agent, which presents its approval
options.C: The policy administrator, which relays the decision
options.D: The resource, which checks the agent's access token itself

questions.key_concept: In Zero Trust, the policy engine decides, the policy administrator relays the decision, and the enforcement point opens or closes the session.
questions.pre_read: Separate the part that decides from the part that sets up the path.
questions.correct_explanation: In NIST's Zero Trust model, the policy engine makes and logs the decision, and the policy administrator carries it out by configuring the enforcement point to open, or later close, the session. The policy engine is the runner-up: it decides, but it does not set up the path itself; together the two form the decision point.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the policy engine does make the decision. But NIST gives the policy administrator the job of telling the enforcement point to open the session.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the agent asked for access. But the requester never instructs the enforcement point; the decision point's components do.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because resources often check tokens. But in Zero Trust the enforcement point guards the resource, acting on the decision point's instructions.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the requester instruct the enforcement point, and D has the resource deciding for itself, which the enforcement point does on instruction.
Final two: C beats A because the policy engine decides, while the policy administrator relays that decision and configures the enforcement point.
Exam cue: engine decides, administrator relays, enforcement point acts; a requester, human or AI agent, never instructs the gate.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 3 (Logical Components of Zero Trust Architecture)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Deciding and enforcing are separate jobs, and every protected resource needs an enforcement point' (notes 4.2.7 Zero Trust Architecture Components). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Network access control
questions.question: A community college's network access control (NAC) policy lists its new badge printers, which cannot do 802.1X sign-in, as approved devices. How should the network technician set up NAC for them as BEST?

options.A: Identify them by profile and give them printing access only
options.B: Admit them to the staff network, since printers hold no data
options.C: Admit them on the staff network by MAC address alone
options.D: Block them from the network until they support 802.1X

questions.key_concept: Devices that cannot do 802.1X are identified by profiling and given only the limited access their job needs, not a free pass.
questions.pre_read: Think about how NAC can still recognize and box in a device that cannot sign in.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy already approves the printers, so the technician sets up how they join: NAC recognizes devices that cannot do 802.1X through profiling, such as device type and behavior, and gives them only the limited access their job requires. MAC-only admission is the runner-up: it is common, but MAC addresses are easy to copy, and putting the printers on the staff network gives a copied address far too much reach.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because printers seem harmless. But badge printers are network computers that attackers can hijack, so they get limited access, not a free pass.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: MAC lists are a common fallback. But MAC addresses are easy to copy, and staff-network access gives a spoofed device far more reach than printing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it keeps NAC strict. But the policy already approves the printers; NAC designs admit such devices with limited access rather than block them.

tips: Eliminate: B gives printers a free pass because they seem harmless, and D blocks devices the policy approves instead of admitting them with limited access.
Final two: A beats C because profiling plus printing-only access limits what a spoofed device could reach, while MAC-only staff access is easy to abuse.
Exam cue: devices that cannot authenticate are still checked and boxed in: identify them, then allow only what their job requires.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.7 (Network Access Control: health checks and limited access for remediation); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Devices that cannot use 802.1X, like printers, are identified by profiling and given limited access, not a free pass' (notes 4.2.8 Network Access Control (NAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. AI development environments
questions.question: A credit bureau's developers must load-test a machine learning pipeline at full volume; the data owner allows no data drawn from real consumers. Which test data should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Live records, with names and account numbers masked
options.B: Synthetic records, generated in the number the test needs
options.C: A few dozen made-up records that developers type in by hand
options.D: Public consumer details gathered from open websites
