questions.key_concept: Masked data still comes from real people; synthetic data copies their patterns without anyone's records, fitting a ban on real data.
questions.pre_read: Ask where each kind of test data originally came from.
questions.correct_explanation: The data owner allows no data drawn from real consumers. Masked records still start as real consumers' records, so they fall outside that rule, while synthetic records are generated to match real volumes and patterns without holding anyone's data. Masking is the runner-up: it hides names and numbers, but the remaining details still belong to real people and can sometimes be linked back to them.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: masking hides direct identifiers. But masked records still come from real consumers, which the data owner has ruled out.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because made-up records hold no one's data. But a few dozen typed-in records cannot load-test a pipeline at full volume.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the details are already public. But they still describe real consumers, which the data owner has ruled out; public does not mean permitted.

tips: Eliminate: C holds no real data but is far too small for a full-volume test, and D still describes real consumers, even if the details are public.
Final two: B beats A because masked records still come from real consumers, which the data owner ruled out; synthetic records never belonged to anyone.
Exam cue: masking hides real people's details; synthetic data never had any. Let the data owner's rule decide which one fits.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-3(2) (System Development Life Cycle | Use of Live or Operational Data); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-8(33) (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles | Minimization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Development uses masked or synthetic data; real sensitive data enters only with the data owner's approval' (notes 4.2.9 Segmenting AI Development Environments). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. AI development environments
questions.question: At a parcel locker company, any developer can copy a model from the artificial intelligence (AI) development segment straight onto production servers. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Scan each model file with antivirus before copying it
options.B: Let production pull the newest model from development hourly
options.C: Move models only through a reviewed, logged release step
options.D: Encrypt each model file, and log every copy to production

questions.key_concept: Trained models are protected assets: they reach production only through a reviewed, logged release, because a tampered model misbehaves while looking normal.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option checks before a model reaches production.
questions.correct_explanation: Trained models are protected assets: a tampered or poisoned model behaves wrongly in production while looking normal. A reviewed, logged release step means someone other than the developer checks each model's source, test results and approval before it moves, so only models from the approved pipeline go live, and every move is traceable. Antivirus scanning is the runner-up: it catches known malware, but a poisoned model holds no malware code to find.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: scanning files is a sensible check. But antivirus looks for known malware, not a model trained to misbehave, so a poisoned model passes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because automation removes manual copying. But it moves every untested change into production automatically, with no review at all.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption protects model files. But it guards secrecy, not integrity, and logging copies does not stop a bad model going live.

tips: Eliminate: B automates the unreviewed path into production, and D protects the model's secrecy, not whether it is safe to run.
Final two: C beats A because a reviewed release confirms where each model came from and how it tested before it goes live; antivirus looks for malware code, which a poisoned model does not contain.
Exam cue: treat trained models like code: changes reach production only through review, approval and a record.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 2.3.3 (Backdoor Poisoning: a model learns to misclassify inputs containing a trigger pattern); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-5 (Access Restrictions for Change)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Trained models and their datasets are protected assets, because tampering with either can poison the model' (notes 4.2.9 Segmenting AI Development Environments). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A yogurt maker's IT manager says virtualization is not one of the five essential cloud characteristics but a technology behind one of them. Which response from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree; it is a technology that makes resource pooling possible
options.B: Disagree; virtualization is what the term resource pooling means
options.C: Disagree; virtualization was added later as a sixth characteristic
options.D: Agree; and rapid elasticity is not one of the five either

questions.key_concept: The five characteristics are self-service, broad network access, pooling, elasticity and measured service; virtualization is a technology that enables pooling.
questions.pre_read: List the five characteristics before judging the claim.
questions.correct_explanation: The five essential characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. Virtualization is not one of them; it is a technology that lets a provider pool hardware among customers. Treating virtualization as resource pooling is the runner-up: the two are closely linked, but pooling is the characteristic, and virtualization is one way to achieve it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: virtualization and pooling are closely linked. But pooling is the characteristic; virtualization is one technology that makes it possible.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because cloud lists vary between vendors. But the definition still names five characteristics, and virtualization is not among them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it starts by agreeing correctly. But rapid elasticity is one of the five: capacity that grows and shrinks quickly with demand.

tips: Eliminate: C invents a sixth characteristic, and D wrongly drops rapid elasticity, which is one of the five.
Final two: A beats B because resource pooling is the characteristic, and virtualization is a technology that makes pooling possible.
Exam cue: the five are self-service, network access, pooling, elasticity and measured service; a technology such as virtualization is never on the list.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: essential characteristics)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Virtualization is one of the five essential characteristics' (exam trap, notes 4.3.1 The Five Essential Characteristics of Cloud Computing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A phone insurance startup's developer says a public container image with millions of downloads is safe to deploy without review. Which reply from the system administrator is MOST accurate?

options.A: Popular images are safe, since many users would spot flaws
options.B: Popularity proves nothing; scan it and use trusted sources
options.C: It is safe once run in a container, not a virtual machine
options.D: Its signature proves it is free of flaws and malware

questions.key_concept: Every public image is outside software: scan it and run only images from trusted, maintained sources; popularity and signatures do not prove it is flaw-free.
questions.pre_read: Ask what download counts and signatures actually prove about an image.
questions.correct_explanation: Download counts show popularity, not safety: public images can carry outdated libraries, malware or secrets, like any outside software. NIST's container guide says to run only images from a maintained set of trusted images and registries, kept updated as flaws emerge. The signature answer is the runner-up: a valid signature proves who published the image and that it was not altered, not that it is flaw-free.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because crowds seem to vet software. But popular images still ship outdated libraries and have carried malware, and no one is accountable for checking.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because containers isolate apps. But containers share the host's kernel, and a flawed or malicious image is just as harmful inside one.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: signatures are a real safeguard. But they prove who published the image and that it is unaltered, not that its contents are free of flaws.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts popularity as proof of safety, and C treats running in a container as a fix for a flawed image.
Final two: B beats D because a signature proves origin and integrity, not that the image is free of flaws; scanning and trusted sources cover that.
Exam cue: secure the template, not just the copy: every image is outside software until it is scanned and pulled from a trusted source.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-190 Section 4.1.5 (Use of untrusted images: maintain a set of trusted images and registries and allow only images from it to run); NIST SP 800-190 Section 3.1.1 (Image vulnerabilities: updates are made upstream in the images, which are then redeployed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Secure the template, not just the copy: harden and patch images, and pull them only from approved sources' (notes 4.3.2 Virtualization and Containers in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A youth orchestra's app runs on a platform as a service (PaaS), and the provider says the runtime version its developers chose will lose support. Which advice from the system administrator is MOST accurate?

options.A: The provider will switch the app to a newer runtime version
options.B: The team must move its own app to a supported runtime version
options.C: The app stays safe while the provider patches the platform
options.D: An unsupported runtime needs no action on an isolated platform

questions.key_concept: In PaaS, the provider patches the runtime versions it supports, but the customer chooses the version its app uses and must move before support ends.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the provider does for a runtime version before and after its support ends.
questions.correct_explanation: In PaaS, the provider patches the runtime versions it supports, but the team chose this version for its code. Once support ends, the provider stops fixing it, so the team must move its app to a supported version and test that the code still works. The provider switching versions itself is the runner-up: providers do patch runtimes, but a new version can break the team's code, so the move is the team's.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the provider patches a runtime while supporting it. But a new version can break the team's code, so the team, which chose it, makes and tests the move.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the provider patches the platform. But once this runtime version loses support, the provider stops patching it, and its new flaws stay open.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because PaaS keeps customers' apps apart. But isolation does not fix flaws in the runtime itself; unsupported software must be replaced or covered by an approved exception.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes the provider keeps patching a version it is retiring, and D treats isolation as a fix for flaws in unsupported software.
Final two: B beats A because the provider patches supported runtimes but does not move the team's code to a new version, which could break it; the team chose the version and makes the move.
Exam cue: in PaaS the provider patches the platform it supports, but the runtime version an app uses is the customer's choice, so moving off an unsupported one is the customer's job.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-22 (Unsupported System Components)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'PaaS customers patch the operating system under their application' (exam trap, notes 4.3.3 Cloud Service Models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Re-angled in the batch 6 fix round to runtime end of support, because its PaaS patching split repeated cc_d4_016.

questions.question: A cartography firm runs its apps across two public cloud providers, and its system owner calls this a hybrid cloud. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: It is hybrid, since any mix of two clouds counts as hybrid
options.B: It is multi-cloud, since both of its providers are public
options.C: It is a community cloud, since two public providers share it
options.D: It is private, since only the firm's staff use its apps

questions.key_concept: Hybrid cloud mixes deployment models, such as private and public; using several public providers is multi-cloud.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the setup mixes kinds of cloud or only counts providers.
questions.correct_explanation: Hybrid cloud joins different deployment models, such as a private cloud with a public one. Using several public providers is multi-cloud: it reduces reliance on any one provider but adds separate consoles and settings to secure. The runner-up stretches hybrid to any mix of clouds, but the word refers to mixing models, not counting providers.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: hybrid does mean a mix. But it mixes deployment models, such as private and public; two public providers make it multi-cloud.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because two parties are involved. But a community cloud is shared by organizations with common needs, not split between providers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because only staff use the apps. But private means infrastructure built for one organization; renting public cloud services is not private.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses two providers with a community of organizations, and D calls rented public services private because only staff use them.
Final two: B beats A because hybrid mixes deployment models, while two public providers is multi-cloud.
Exam cue: hybrid counts models, multi-cloud counts providers; one setup can be both, but two public clouds alone is only multi-cloud.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: deployment models)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Hybrid cloud and multi-cloud mean the same thing' (exam trap, notes 4.3.4 Cloud Deployment Models). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A distillery is moving payroll from its infrastructure as a service (IaaS) virtual machines to a software as a service (SaaS) product. Which duty can its system administrator MOST clearly drop?

options.A: Patching the operating system and payroll software
options.B: Deciding which staff accounts may view salary records
options.C: Setting the payroll service's sharing and export options
options.D: Answering to staff if salary records are ever exposed

questions.key_concept: Moving from IaaS to SaaS shifts patching of the operating system and application to the provider; data, accounts, access and settings stay with the customer.
questions.pre_read: Sort each duty into the provider's platform or the customer's own use of it.
questions.correct_explanation: Moving from IaaS to SaaS hands the provider every technical layer, including the operating system and the payroll application, so patching them leaves the distillery's list. Configuration stays with the customer in every model, which makes the sharing and export settings the runner-up: the provider supplies the options, but the distillery chooses and maintains them.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because SaaS providers run the service. But deciding who may see salary records is account and access management, which stays with the customer.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the provider does build the sharing options. But choosing and maintaining the settings stays with the customer in every service model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider runs the service. But accountability for its staff's data stays with the distillery, even when a provider does the work.

tips: Eliminate: B is access management and D is accountability for the data, and both stay with the customer in every model.
Final two: A beats C because SaaS hands the provider the operating system and application, while service settings remain the customer's to choose.
Exam cue: moving up from IaaS to SaaS shifts patching to the provider; data, accounts, access and settings never move.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models); NIST SP 800-144 Section 2.3 (Outsourcing and Accountability)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The provider owns security of the cloud; the customer owns security in the cloud' (notes 4.3.5 The Shared Responsibility Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.3 Cloud security. Cloud roles and agreements
questions.question: A party supplies chain's draft cloud contract says the provider will report breaches affecting the firm's data 'when practical'. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: A right to inspect the provider's data centers in person
options.B: A set deadline for the provider to report such breaches
options.C: Monthly uptime reports against the service level agreement
options.D: A clause moving all accountability for breaches to the provider

questions.key_concept: A cloud contract should set a deadline for the provider to report breaches, so the customer can meet its own notice duties.
questions.pre_read: Name the gap in the contract, then find the clause that closes that gap.
questions.correct_explanation: The gap is vague breach reporting: 'when practical' could mean weeks. A set deadline lets the firm investigate and meet its own legal notice duties in time. A right to inspect data centers is the runner-up: it adds assurance about controls, but it does nothing about when the firm hears of a breach, and large providers usually offer independent reports instead.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: inspection rights are a real contract safeguard. But they test controls; they do not fix when the provider must tell the firm about a breach.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because SLA reports are the best-known contract term. But uptime reports cover availability, not when the provider must tell the firm about a breach.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider holds the data. But accountability for the firm's data stays with the firm, whatever the contract says.

tips: Eliminate: C adds uptime reports, which cover availability rather than breaches, and D tries to move accountability, which stays with the firm whatever the contract says.
Final two: B beats A because the gap is when the firm hears of a breach; inspection rights test controls but leave reporting as vague as before.
Exam cue: match the clause to the gap: a reporting deadline for breaches, an SLA for uptime, independent reports for assurance, exit terms for deletion.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-05 (requirements to address cybersecurity risks in supply chains are established, prioritized and integrated into contracts and other agreements with suppliers); NIST SP 800-144 Section 2.3 (Outsourcing and Accountability)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Contracts should set service targets and cover data location, breach notification and deleting data at exit' (notes 4.3.6 Cloud Roles and Agreements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A music school will move all its file shares to cloud storage next month, and nobody knows which folders hold student records. What should the system administrator propose FIRST?

options.A: Encrypt every folder at the strongest level, then move it all
options.B: Move everything now, and let data owners sort it afterward
options.C: Have the data owners classify the folders before anything moves
options.D: Ask the provider to label the sensitive folders as they move

questions.key_concept: Classify data before it moves to the cloud, so the most sensitive gets the strongest controls or stays out; data owners set the classification.
questions.pre_read: Ask what has to be known before anyone can choose the right controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Data owners decide classification, and classifying before the move shows which folders hold student records, so each class gets the right controls, such as tighter access and encryption, or stays out of the cloud. Encrypting everything is the runner-up: it protects storage, but without knowing what is sensitive, access rules, sharing settings and the choice of what should move remain guesses.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: encryption is a sound control for cloud data. But it does not tell anyone which folders need tighter access or should not move at all.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it keeps the project on schedule. But sensitive records would land in the cloud with whatever settings they happen to get.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because providers offer labeling tools. But deciding how sensitive the school's data is belongs to the school's data owners, not the provider.

tips: Eliminate: B moves sensitive records before anyone knows where they are, and D hands classification, a customer duty, to the provider.
Final two: C beats A because classification decides which controls each folder needs, while blanket encryption leaves access and placement decisions unmade.
Exam cue: in the cloud, the data is always the customer's job, and protecting it starts with knowing what it is: classify before you move.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-05 (assets are prioritized based on classification, criticality, resources and impact on the mission); NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.7 (Data Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Classify data before it moves, so the most sensitive gets the strongest controls or stays out' (notes 4.3.7 Protecting Data in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bus tour firm's team made a storage bucket of passenger lists public, and it leaked; the data owner blames the cloud provider for allowing public buckets. What is the system administrator's MOST accurate reply?

options.A: The provider shares the fault, as it should block public buckets
options.B: The provider caused it, since it runs the storage service
options.C: Bucket access is a customer setting, so the firm caused it
options.D: It depends on the service model, which the firm must check

questions.key_concept: Storage permissions are a customer setting in every service model, so a bucket the customer made public is the customer's misconfiguration to prevent and catch.
questions.pre_read: Ask who chose the bucket's access setting.
questions.correct_explanation: Storage permissions are a customer setting in every cloud service model. The provider offers public and private options; the firm's team chose public, so the leak came from the firm's misconfiguration, which baselines and posture checks such as CSPM exist to catch. Shared fault is the runner-up: providers do offer safeguards against public buckets, but offering the option does not make the provider responsible for how the firm set it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: providers do offer settings that block public buckets. But the firm's team chose the public setting, and that choice is the customer's part.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the provider runs the service. But running the storage is not the same as setting who may read each bucket.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because many cloud duties shift with the service model. But who may read stored data is a customer setting in every model, so the answer does not change.

tips: Eliminate: B blames the provider for a setting the firm chose, and D thinks the answer changes with the service model, when storage access is the customer's in every model.
Final two: C beats A because who may read a bucket is the customer's setting in every model; provider safeguards help, but the firm set it public.
Exam cue: the provider supplies the settings and the customer chooses them; a public bucket is a customer misconfiguration.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-144 Section 2.3 (Outsourcing and Accountability); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-01 (configuration management practices are established and applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'If a storage bucket was public, the provider caused the breach' (exam trap, notes 4.3.8 Cloud Misconfiguration, CSPM and CASB). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A guided-hike company hosts a translation model on infrastructure as a service (IaaS) virtual machines and uses a managed chatbot service; both run the same flawed serving software. Which patching is MOST clearly the company's?

options.A: Both copies, since the company uses each of them
options.B: Only its own copy, since the company installed it
options.C: Neither copy, since the provider runs the whole cloud
options.D: Only the managed service's, since it faces the internet

questions.key_concept: AI follows the service model: providers patch managed AI services, but customers patch software they install on IaaS machines.
questions.pre_read: Place each copy of the software in the stack, then ask who runs it.
questions.correct_explanation: The service model decides who patches. On IaaS the provider's share stops at the hardware and virtualization layer, so serving software the company installed on its virtual machines is the company's to patch. In the managed chatbot service, the provider runs the model and its software and patches that copy. Patching both is the runner-up: the company relies on each copy, but it has no access to the provider's software, or duty to patch it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the company depends on both copies. But in a managed service the provider runs and patches the serving software, which the company cannot reach.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the provider runs the cloud under both. But on IaaS its share stops at the hardware and virtualization layer, below the software the company installed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because internet-facing systems are often patched first. But who patches depends on who runs the software, not on how exposed it is, and the provider runs the managed service.

tips: Eliminate: C hands software the company installed to the provider, whose IaaS share stops at the virtualization layer, and D decides by exposure instead of by who runs the software.
Final two: B beats A because the managed chatbot's serving software is the provider's to patch; the company patches only the copy it installed on IaaS.
Exam cue: AI follows the service model: the provider patches a managed AI service, and you patch any model software you install on IaaS.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The split follows the service model; data and access always stay with the customer' (notes 4.3.9 Shared Responsibility for AI Workloads). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Re-angled in the batch 6 fix round to contrast a managed AI service with a self-hosted model, because the IaaS patching lesson repeated cc_d4_043.

questions.question: A guitar maker's procedure has the system administrator enable logging on new cloud services; its managed artificial intelligence (AI) service can log prompts and replies, but logging is off. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Turn on logging, with read access for named staff only
options.B: Turn on logging for replies only, leaving prompts unrecorded
options.C: Keep logging off, since the provider monitors its platform
options.D: Turn on logging, and give every staff account read access

questions.key_concept: Watching its own use of a cloud AI service is the customer's job: turn logging on and protect the logs, which can hold sensitive prompts.
questions.pre_read: Check what the procedure assigns, then think about what the logs will contain.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedure assigns enabling logging to the administrator, and in shared responsibility the customer watches its own use of a cloud service, AI included. Prompts show what staff sent and any misuse, so they are logged too, and because they may hold sensitive details, read access is limited to named staff. Logging replies only is the runner-up: it records less sensitive text, but it hides what staff actually sent.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: leaving prompts out records less sensitive text. But prompts show what staff sent and any misuse; limiting who reads the logs protects them without leaving them unrecorded.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the provider does monitor its platform. But that covers the provider's systems, not how the company's staff use the service.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it turns logging on as required. But prompts and replies can hold sensitive data, so wide read access creates a new leak.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves the company blind to its own AI use, and D turns logging on but exposes the sensitive log contents to everyone.
Final two: A beats B because prompts show what staff sent and any misuse; limiting who reads the logs protects them without leaving them unrecorded.
Exam cue: in any cloud model, watching your own use is your job; turn logging on and protect the logs, since they hold the same data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.4 (the functionality and behavior of the AI system are monitored when in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Training data and tuned models are customer assets needing access control, encryption and logging' (notes 4.3.9 Shared Responsibility for AI Workloads). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bowling alley chain's network technician turns on Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) validation at its DNS resolver. What does this MOST directly add to staff name lookups?

options.A: Encryption that hides each lookup from anyone on the network path
options.B: Blocking of lookups for domains known to host harmful content
options.C: Signature checks that reveal forged or altered DNS answers
options.D: Faster answers, by caching names on a server near each venue

questions.key_concept: DNSSEC signs DNS answers so a validating resolver can spot forgery or tampering; it does not encrypt lookups.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a forged DNS answer would do to a device, and what a digital signature can prove.
questions.correct_explanation: DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS data, so a resolver that validates them can tell when an answer was forged or altered on the way, and refuse it. It protects integrity and the source's authenticity only. Encryption is the runner-up: it is a real DNS protection, but it comes from encrypted DNS, such as DNS over TLS, while DNSSEC answers still travel readable.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: lookups can be encrypted. But that is encrypted DNS, such as DNS over TLS; DNSSEC signs answers and leaves them readable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because some resolvers do filter bad domains. But that is protective DNS filtering, a separate service; DNSSEC only proves answers are genuine.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because resolvers do cache answers. But caching is a speed feature that works with or without DNSSEC, which adds signatures.

tips: Eliminate: B describes protective DNS filtering, and D describes caching; neither is what DNSSEC adds.
Final two: C beats A because DNSSEC signs answers so tampering shows, but it does not encrypt them; encrypted DNS does that.
Exam cue: signatures prove integrity and origin, not secrecy; an option that says a signing control hides data is mixing up the two.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-81 Rev. 3 Section 3.8 (DNSSEC Signing Considerations for Authoritative Service: DNSSEC adds source authentication and integrity protection but does not protect confidentiality); NIST SP 800-81 Rev. 3 Section 1.1 (Domain Name Systems: translating domain names into IP addresses is called name resolution)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) sign DNS answers so tampering can be detected; they do not encrypt them' (notes 4.1.1 Network Building Blocks). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A puppet theater's security analyst says Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 (WPA3) also protects payroll data on the cable beyond the access point. Which reply from the network technician is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree; WPA3 keeps the data encrypted until the server receives it
options.B: Disagree; WPA3 works at layer 3, so it covers routed traffic only
options.C: Disagree; the cable is inside the office, so it needs no encryption
options.D: Disagree; WPA3 covers only the radio hop, so the app needs TLS

questions.key_concept: Wi-Fi encryption such as WPA3 protects only the radio link to the access point; end-to-end protection needs a higher-layer protocol such as TLS.
questions.pre_read: Picture the path the payroll data takes, hop by hop, and which layer each protection works at.
questions.correct_explanation: WPA3 encrypts frames at layer 2, between the laptop and the access point only. The access point decrypts them before passing them onto the wired network, so payroll data on the cable is readable unless the app itself uses TLS, which protects it end to end. Saying the cable needs no encryption is the runner-up: it rejects the claim, but trusting the internal network is the mistake.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because WPA3 is strong encryption. But the access point decrypts each frame, so the data crosses the cable unprotected unless the app adds TLS.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because WPA3 is a network setting. But Wi-Fi encryption works at layer 2, the data link layer, not at layer 3.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it rightly rejects the claim. But inside does not mean trusted; anyone on the wired network could capture the readable data.

tips: Eliminate: A fails because the access point decrypts each frame, and B puts Wi-Fi encryption at layer 3 instead of layer 2.
Final two: D beats C because inside does not mean trusted; once WPA3 ends at the access point, only TLS keeps payroll data protected.
Exam cue: ask where each encryption starts and stops; link-layer encryption protects one hop, while TLS protects the whole conversation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1 Section 8.1.1 (WiFi Data Link Protection); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-8(1) (Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity | Cryptographic Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Wi-Fi encrypts at layer 2, IP Security (IPsec) at layer 3, and Transport Layer Security (TLS) above layer 4' (notes 4.1.2 The OSI Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An opera house's phone system vendor says its calls use the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) because resending late audio is pointless. Which reply from the network technician is MOST accurate?

options.A: Disagree; UDP lacks delivery checks, so the calls should move to TCP
options.B: Agree; losing a sound packet matters less than delaying the call
options.C: Disagree; UDP resends lost packets in the same way that TCP does
options.D: Agree; UDP also encrypts each packet, which keeps the calls private

questions.key_concept: UDP skips delivery checks and resends, which suits live voice and video where late data is useless; that is a design choice, not a flaw.
questions.pre_read: Compare what TCP and UDP each do when a packet goes missing, and what a live call needs.
questions.correct_explanation: UDP sends each packet once, with no handshake or resend. On a live call, a resent sound packet would arrive too late to play, so a tiny gap beats a stalled call; that is why voice and video use UDP. Moving calls to TCP is the runner-up: its reliability sounds safer, but its resends and waits make live audio lag, and neither protocol encrypts.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: TCP does check delivery. But on live calls its resends and waits cause lag; UDP's missing checks are a design choice, not a weakness.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because both are transport protocols. But UDP has no acknowledgments and never resends; that is its main difference from TCP.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because some call systems do encrypt audio. But UDP itself adds no encryption; calls need a protocol on top, such as Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP).

tips: Eliminate: C claims UDP resends lost packets, and D claims UDP encrypts them; it does neither.
Final two: B beats A because live audio cannot wait for resends; UDP suits calls, and security comes from protocols on top.
Exam cue: match the protocol to the job; TCP for complete, ordered data, UDP for speed where late data is useless.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-94 Section 4.1.2 (Transport Layer: when loss of some application data is not a concern, such as streaming audio and video, UDP is typically used)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The User Datagram Protocol (UDP) sends each datagram alone, with no delivery check, which suits name lookups, voice and video' (notes 4.1.3 The TCP/IP Model, TCP and UDP). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A citrus grower's laptops use Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6), which its firewall filters as fully as IPv4, but the security analyst's alert rules match only IPv4. What should the analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Extend the alert rules so that they also match IPv6 addresses
options.B: Keep the alert rules, since the firewall already filters IPv6
options.C: Rely on IPv6's built-in IPsec to block harmful traffic instead
options.D: Keep the alert rules, since private IPv4 addresses hide the laptops

questions.key_concept: Prevention and detection must each cover both IPv4 and IPv6; a firewall that filters IPv6 does not make IPv4-only alerts see it.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the firewall decides from what the alert rules can see.
questions.correct_explanation: The firewall decides which IPv6 traffic may pass, but alert rules are how the analyst spots attacks hiding in allowed traffic. Rules that match only IPv4 leave every IPv6 connection unwatched, so an attack over IPv6 raises no alert. Extending the rules closes the gap. Relying on the firewall is the runner-up: filtering and detection are separate layers, and a firewall does not judge whether allowed traffic is an attack.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the firewall does filter IPv6. But filtering only decides what passes; spotting attacks inside allowed IPv6 traffic needs alert rules that can see it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IPv6 was designed with IPsec in mind. But IPsec must be set up, and it encrypts traffic rather than detecting attacks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because private addresses are not routed on the internet. But they filter and detect nothing, and IPv6 traffic bypasses IPv4 rules anyway.

tips: Eliminate: C treats IPv6's IPsec as automatic protection, and D treats private IPv4 addresses as a security control.
Final two: A beats B because the firewall only decides what passes; attacks inside allowed IPv6 traffic need alert rules that can see IPv6.
Exam cue: check prevention and detection separately for each IP version; covering IPv6 in one layer does not cover it in the other.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-119 Section 6.1.1 (Attacker Community: IPv6 traffic may not be detectable by security controls that do not monitor it, so make them both IPv4 and IPv6 aware); NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 4.1.2 (IPv6: filter IPv6 traffic as fully as IPv4)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Many systems enable IPv6 by default, so rules and monitoring must cover both versions' (notes 4.1.4 IPv4 and IPv6). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A tea merchant's system administrator says moving its wholesale order form to Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) will not stop buyers' uploaded files from carrying malware. Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Disagree; TLS scans each uploaded file before storing it
options.B: Disagree; harmful files cannot travel to a site on port 443
options.C: Agree; HTTPS protects files in transit, not what they contain
options.D: Agree, but HTTPS stops them if plain HTTP gets switched off

questions.key_concept: HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server; it does not check what the data contains, so uploads still need malware scanning.
questions.pre_read: Separate protecting data on its way from checking what the data contains.
questions.correct_explanation: The administrator is right. HTTPS wraps web traffic in TLS, so files cannot be read or altered on the way, but it carries an infected file as faithfully as a clean one. Uploads still need their own checks on the server, such as malware scanning and allowed file types. Turning off plain HTTP is the runner-up: it is good practice for data in transit, but infected files arrive through HTTPS anyway.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because TLS does protect the upload. But it only encrypts the file in transit; it never checks whether the file is safe.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because HTTPS uses port 443. But a port is only a number; an infected file reaches port 443 just like a clean one.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: plain HTTP should be turned off too. But infected files arrive through HTTPS like real orders, so closing HTTP stops none of them.

tips: Eliminate: A has TLS scanning files, and B treats port 443 as a barrier; TLS only encrypts, and a port is just a number.
Final two: C beats D because an infected file rides inside the encrypted channel; closing plain HTTP protects transit, not content.
Exam cue: encryption in transit protects the pipe, not what flows through it; content needs its own checks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-8(1) (Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity | Cryptographic Protection); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-3 (Malicious Code Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Encryption protects data in transit, but every open port is still a way in, so expose only what the business needs' (notes 4.1.5 Ports, Protocols and Secure Alternatives). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A furniture studio's VPN serves outside support; its file server exposes ports 445 (office file sharing) and 3389 (a vendor's monthly remote desktop) to the internet. What should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep both ports open, moving remote desktop to a high port
options.B: Keep both ports open, since staff already connect over the VPN
options.C: Close both ports, and give the vendor remote desktop over the VPN
options.D: Close port 445, and allow 3389 only from the vendor's own addresses

questions.key_concept: Expose only what the business needs: close services nobody outside uses, and route occasional remote access through a VPN rather than an open port.
questions.pre_read: Ask who actually needs each port from the internet, and how often.
questions.correct_explanation: Nobody outside needs file sharing, so port 445 should close, and remote desktop should not face the internet either; the vendor can connect through the studio's VPN, which already serves outside support and adds a verified sign-in before the server is reachable. Allowing 3389 from the vendor's addresses is the runner-up: it narrows exposure, but remote desktop still faces the internet, guarded only by the server's own login.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fewer scanners probe high ports. But scanners find services on any port in minutes, and both services stay exposed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the studio already has a VPN. But a VPN protects only traffic that uses it; ports left open still face the whole internet.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it closes file sharing and narrows remote desktop. But remote desktop still faces the internet, guarded only by the server's own login.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on an unusual port, and B assumes a VPN protects ports that stay open; scanners find any port, and the VPN covers only its own traffic.
Final two: C beats D because a monthly vendor visit fits the VPN; an address-limited remote desktop port still faces the internet directly.
Exam cue: sort exposed ports by who uses them; close what only on-site staff need, and an address list still leaves a service facing the internet.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-7 (Least Functionality); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-17 (Remote Access)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is reached through a VPN or gateway with MFA, and Server Message Block (SMB) never faces the internet' (notes 4.1.5 Ports, Protocols and Secure Alternatives). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A wildlife charity lets volunteers join its virtual private network (VPN) from their own laptops, and every sign-in already uses multifactor authentication (MFA). Which added control should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Stronger encryption on the tunnel between laptops and the office
options.B: A health check of each laptop before its VPN session is allowed
options.C: Split tunneling, so that less volunteer traffic crosses the VPN
options.D: A second MFA prompt every hour while volunteers stay connected

questions.key_concept: A VPN protects the path, not the device: personal laptops need a health check before they connect, because malware travels through the tunnel.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the tunnel protects, and what MFA already covers here.
questions.correct_explanation: MFA already proves who is signing in, and the tunnel already encrypts the path. What neither checks is the laptop: an unpatched or infected personal device would carry malware straight into the network through the tunnel. A health check before each session closes that gap. Hourly MFA prompts are the runner-up: they recheck the person, but an infected laptop passes every prompt.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a VPN is about encryption. But the tunnel is already encrypted; stronger encryption does nothing about malware on the laptop.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it eases the load on the VPN. But internet traffic then skips the charity's filtering and monitoring, which weakens protection.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: rechecking identity helps against stolen sessions. But it proves only who is there; an infected laptop passes every prompt.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens a tunnel that is already encrypted, and C sends traffic around the charity's filtering and monitoring.
Final two: B beats D because MFA already covers identity; the open risk is the personal laptop itself, which only a device check addresses.
Exam cue: when identity and the tunnel are already covered, look for the gap that is left; for personal laptops, that gap is the device's own health.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-46 Rev. 2 Section 2.1 (Vulnerabilities, Threats, and Security Controls: infected client devices); NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.7 (Network Access Control: health checks and limited access for remediation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A VPN protects the path, not the device at either end' (notes 4.1.6 Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A film studio's producer phones the network technician demanding a firewall port opened today for a vendor's upload; procedure routes firewall changes to the system owner for approval. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Open the port now, and tell the system owner afterward
options.B: Submit a change request for the system owner to approve
options.C: Open the port for one day, since it is just temporary
options.D: Ask the producer to approve the change in writing first

questions.key_concept: Firewall rules change only through change management; a requester's urgency does not replace the system owner's approval.
questions.pre_read: Check who the procedure says approves firewall changes.
questions.correct_explanation: The procedure sends firewall changes to the system owner, so the technician submits a change request and lets the owner decide; urgent changes can still move quickly through that route. Getting the producer's written approval is the runner-up: it looks careful, but the producer is the requester, not the firewall's owner, so their signature authorizes nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the upload is urgent. But a live edit outside change management skips the owner's review, and telling the owner afterward does not fix that.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a short-lived rule sounds low risk. But temporary rules still need approval, and they are easily left open.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: written approval looks careful. But the producer is the requester, not the system owner the procedure names.

tips: Eliminate: A edits the firewall outside change management, and C assumes a temporary rule needs no approval.
Final two: B beats D because only the system owner can approve the change; the producer's signature comes from the wrong person.
Exam cue: the person asking for a change is not the person who approves it; find the approver the procedure names, however urgent the request.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-01 (configuration management practices are established and applied)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Allow only what the business needs with the narrowest rule, deny the rest, and change rules only through change management' (notes 4.1.7 Firewalls: Ports and Applications). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: In a magazine publisher's penetration test, a laptop reaches other laptops' file-sharing ports directly through the office switch. Which control should the network technician propose as BEST to stop this?

options.A: Host-based firewalls that refuse unrequested connections
options.B: Stricter file-sharing rules on the edge firewall
options.C: An intrusion detection system fed a copy of switch traffic
options.D: File sharing moved to an unusual, high port number

questions.key_concept: A network firewall filters only traffic that passes through it; host-based firewalls protect each machine from neighbors on the same subnet.
questions.pre_read: Trace the path the probes take, and which devices they actually cross.
questions.correct_explanation: Laptops on the same subnet talk directly through the switch, so their traffic never reaches the edge firewall. A host-based firewall runs on each laptop and can refuse connections nobody requested, whatever their source. Stricter edge rules are the runner-up: they sound like the natural fix, but the edge firewall never sees this traffic at all.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: tighter firewall rules sound like the natural fix. But laptop-to-laptop traffic on one subnet never passes the edge firewall.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it would reveal the probes. But a passive intrusion detection system only alerts; it cannot block the traffic itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fewer probes target unusual ports. But scanners check every port, and a new number blocks nothing.

tips: Eliminate: C only detects, since a passive IDS cannot block, and D relies on an unusual port number.
Final two: A beats B because traffic between laptops on one subnet never reaches the edge firewall; only a control on each laptop sees it.
Exam cue: a firewall can only filter what passes through it; for traffic between neighbors, put the control on the hosts.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.2.1 (Host-Based Firewalls and Personal Firewalls: protection from hosts on the same subnet that no network firewall separates); NIST SP 800-215 Section 2.1 (Limitations of Network Perimeter-based Protections: east-west traffic stays within the local network)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Host-based firewalls run on each computer and keep protecting laptops away from the office' (notes 4.1.7 Firewalls: Ports and Applications). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. Host and network sensors
questions.question: A ski resort's lift-gate card readers cannot run any added software, and the security analyst wants to spot suspicious traffic around them. Which intrusion detection system (IDS) setup should the analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: A network IDS sensor placed at the internet edge
options.B: A network IDS sensor watching the readers' own segment
options.C: A host-based IDS agent on the server the readers report to
options.D: A network IDS sensor watching the staff office segment

questions.key_concept: A network-based IDS watches a whole segment's traffic, so it can cover devices that cannot run a host agent.
questions.pre_read: Consider where each sensor sits and which traffic it can actually see.
questions.correct_explanation: A host-based IDS needs an agent on the device it protects, and the readers cannot run one. A network-based sensor on the readers' segment sees every reader's traffic, whichever system it talks to. An agent on the server is the runner-up: it is a real host-based option, but it sees only traffic that reaches that one server, not readers talking to anything else.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because edge sensors are common. But reader traffic to internal systems never crosses the internet edge, so most of it goes unseen.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it uses a host agent where one can run. But it sees only traffic reaching that server, missing readers talking to other systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the office segment holds the most users. But the readers' traffic never crosses it, so the sensor sees none of it.

tips: Eliminate: A and D watch segments the readers' traffic mostly never crosses: the internet edge and the staff office.
Final two: B beats C because a sensor on the readers' segment sees all their traffic; an agent on one server sees only what reaches it.
Exam cue: when devices cannot run agents, watch them from the network, and pick the sensor whose position sees the traffic in question.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-94 Section 4.5 (Summary: a network-based IDPS monitors network traffic for particular network segments or devices); NIST SP 800-94 Section 7.1.1 (Typical Components: most host-based IDPSs have agents installed on the hosts of interest)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A network-based system watches traffic on a segment; a host-based system watches one computer's activity, logs and files' (notes 4.1.8 Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A currency exchange's owner says a false positive does more harm on its intrusion prevention system (IPS) than on its intrusion detection system (IDS). Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree; an IPS false positive blocks traffic, an IDS one alerts
options.B: Disagree; an IDS false positive also blocks the traffic it flags
options.C: Disagree; on both, a false positive only wastes analyst time
options.D: Agree; an IPS false positive also lets the real attack through

questions.key_concept: An IPS sits inline, so a false positive blocks genuine traffic; an IDS gets a copy, so its false positive only raises an alert.
questions.pre_read: Picture where each system sits in the traffic path.
questions.correct_explanation: An IPS sits inline, so every packet passes through it; when it wrongly flags genuine traffic, such as a rate feed, it blocks that traffic and the business feels it. An IDS works on a copy of the traffic, so its false positive costs an analyst's time but stops nothing. The runner-up, that a false positive only wastes analyst time, is true of the IDS alone.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because both systems flag the same activity. But an IDS works on a copy of the traffic, so it alerts without blocking anything.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: an IDS false positive does only cost analyst time. But an inline IPS also blocks the genuine traffic it misjudges.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both are detection errors. But letting a real attack through is a false negative; a false positive flags harmless traffic.

tips: Eliminate: B has the IDS blocking, though it works on a copy of the traffic, and D describes a false negative, which misses a real attack.
Final two: A beats C because the IPS sits inline; its wrong verdict blocks genuine traffic, not just an analyst's time.
Exam cue: ask where a tool sits; inline tools act on their mistakes, so their false positives disrupt the business, while passive tools only alert.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-94 Section 4.2.2 (Network Architectures and Sensor Locations: inline versus passive sensors); NIST SP 800-94 Section 2.2 (Key Functions of IDPS Technologies: a false positive flags benign activity, and altering the configuration to improve detection accuracy is called tuning)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'An IPS sits inline, so every packet passes through it, and a wrong block stops legitimate business traffic' (notes 4.1.8 Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. AI in traffic monitoring
questions.question: A children's museum's trial of an artificial intelligence (AI) traffic monitor would upload full packet captures, including unencrypted payroll traffic, to the vendor's cloud. Which setup should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Send full captures, since the upload is encrypted in transit
options.B: Skip the trial, since any data sent to an AI service leaks
options.C: Send only flow records, such as timing, volume and addresses
options.D: Send full captures, under a contract barring vendor reuse

questions.key_concept: Send an AI service only the data it needs: traffic models work from flow patterns, so full captures with sensitive content add risk without need.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model actually needs to see to spot unusual traffic.
questions.correct_explanation: AI traffic monitors learn from patterns such as timing, volume and destinations, which flow records carry without the content. Full captures would hand the vendor readable payroll data for no detection benefit, so sending less is the better design. A contract barring reuse is the runner-up: it limits what the vendor may do, but the payroll data would still leave the museum.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the upload would be encrypted. But encryption protects the trip only; the vendor still receives readable payroll data.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because uploads can leak data. But flow records give the model what it needs without sensitive content, so the trial can go ahead.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a contract does limit how the vendor may use the data. But payroll content would still leave the museum when flow records would do.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on encryption in transit, which still delivers payroll data to the vendor, and B drops a trial that minimized data makes safe.
Final two: C beats D because the model needs only patterns; sending less beats promises about what is sent.
Exam cue: a contract limits what a vendor may do with data it holds; sending less means it never holds it. When a lighter feed does the job, choose the lighter feed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-8(33) (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles | Minimization); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-4(13) (System Monitoring | Analyze Traffic and Event Patterns)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The model learns a traffic baseline (who talks to whom, when and how much) and scores new activity against it' (notes 4.1.9 AI in Traffic Monitoring, IDS and Firewalls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. AI in traffic monitoring
questions.question: A stock photo agency's artificial intelligence (AI) monitor, tuned in alert-only mode, can now cut off devices it scores as risky, payment servers included. Which setup should the security manager choose as BEST?

options.A: Auto-block laptops; analysts confirm any block of a server
options.B: Auto-block any device it scores as risky, the servers included
options.C: Let the vendor's defaults decide which devices it may block
options.D: Auto-block devices it scores in its highest risk band

questions.key_concept: Let AI act automatically where a wrong block costs little, and keep a person in the loop before high-impact blocks.
questions.pre_read: Weigh the cost of a wrong automatic block on each kind of device.
questions.correct_explanation: AI scores still produce false positives, so the impact of a wrong block decides how much automation is safe. Cutting off a laptop is cheap to undo; cutting off payment servers stops the business, so those blocks wait for an analyst to confirm. Blocking only the highest scores is the runner-up: it cuts false positives, but it sets confidence, not impact, and a rare wrong block of a payment server is still an outage.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because automatic blocking contains threats fastest. But AI scores include false positives, and one wrong block of the payment servers halts the business.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor knows the product. But only the agency knows which of its systems are critical, so it must set the limits.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a high score threshold does cut false positives. But it still lets the AI cut off payment servers alone, and even top scores are sometimes wrong.

tips: Eliminate: B automates every block though AI scores include false positives, and C hands the agency's own risk decision to vendor defaults.
Final two: A beats D because a score threshold sets confidence, not impact; even a top-band false positive on payment servers stops the business.
Exam cue: match automation to impact; the costlier a wrong action, the more a person should confirm it, however confident the tool.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 3.2 (roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems are defined); NIST SP 800-94 Section 2.2 (Key Functions of IDPS Technologies: a false positive flags benign activity, and altering the configuration to improve detection accuracy is called tuning)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Scores feed intrusion detection system (IDS) alerts or analyst queues; high-impact automatic blocks get a human check first' (notes 4.1.9 AI in Traffic Monitoring, IDS and Firewalls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A climbing gym's owner plans to hide the staff Wi-Fi network's name as its main protection, instead of upgrading the access point. Which reply from the IT technician is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree; hiding works well with a long and random name
options.B: Agree; hiding the name also stops copycat networks posing as it
options.C: Disagree; hidden names still show in traffic, so tools reveal them
options.D: Disagree; add MAC filtering too, and then hiding will be enough

questions.key_concept: Hiding a Wi-Fi network's name adds little, because the name still appears in connection traffic; strong encryption and sign-in do the real work.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a listening device can still see when a network's name is not announced.
questions.correct_explanation: A hidden network's name still travels whenever devices connect, so free wireless tools reveal it within minutes; hiding is not protection. Real protection comes from strong encryption and sign-in, such as WPA3 on an access point that supports it. Adding MAC filtering is the runner-up: it sounds like a second layer, but MAC addresses are easy to copy from the same traffic.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because long, random names are hard to guess. But nobody needs to guess; devices reveal the name each time they connect.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a hidden name seems harder to copy. But attackers learn it from traffic and can still set up a look-alike network.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it adds a second control. But MAC addresses are easy to copy, so two weak controls together are still weak.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes attackers must guess the hidden name, and B assumes hiding blocks look-alike networks; the name leaks in normal traffic.
Final two: C beats D because MAC filtering is just as easy to get around; encryption and sign-in do the real work.
Exam cue: on wireless, prefer controls an attacker cannot simply watch and copy; names and MAC addresses travel in the clear.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-94 Section 5.1.2 (WLAN Components: SSIDs are broadcast in plaintext, so any listening device can learn them, and MAC addresses are relatively trivial to spoof); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-18(1) (Wireless Access | Authentication and Encryption)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Guest Wi-Fi belongs on its own segment; hiding the network name or filtering by media access control (MAC) address adds little' (notes 4.1.10 Wireless Security: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. Embedded and control systems
questions.question: A city's traffic team is ranking security goals for the controllers that run its traffic signals. Which goal should the security analyst place FIRST?

options.A: Preventing unsafe signal states, such as green lights both ways
options.B: Keeping the signal timing plans confidential from outsiders
options.C: Keeping every controller running without any interruption
options.D: Patching every controller as quickly as the office laptops

questions.key_concept: In industrial and control systems, people's safety comes first, then keeping the process running, then protecting the data.
questions.pre_read: Think about what can go wrong in the physical world when a controller misbehaves.
questions.correct_explanation: Controllers that move physical things can hurt people, so safety comes first: a junction must never show conflicting greens, whatever else happens. Keeping the process running comes next, and data confidentiality after that. Keeping every controller running is the runner-up: availability matters greatly in control systems, but a signal that keeps running in an unsafe state is worse than one that stops.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because confidentiality leads in many office systems. But in control systems, safety and the process come well before secret timing plans.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: availability ranks high in control systems. But safety ranks higher; a controller running in an unsafe state is worse than one that stops.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fast patching protects laptops. But untested patches can crash controllers, so patches are tested and scheduled instead.

tips: Eliminate: B puts data secrecy first, an office priority, and D patches controllers like laptops, which can crash them.
Final two: A beats C because safety outranks availability; a controller that keeps running unsafely is worse than one that stops.
Exam cue: when systems move physical things, rank people's safety first, then the process, then the data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 2.4 (Comparing OT and IT System Security: human safety is paramount, followed by protection of the process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'With systems that move physical things, protect people first, then keep the process running' (notes 4.1.11 Embedded Systems and Industrial Control Systems). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An office tower's landlord is buying networked lighting controllers that will stay in service for about ten years. Which feature should the network technician rank as MOST important?

options.A: A tamper-resistant case that blocks hands-on access to its debug ports
options.B: One admin password the installer sets the same on every unit
options.C: Central control of every unit through the landlord's own app
options.D: Signed firmware updates from the maker for the units' whole life

questions.key_concept: For connected devices that stay in service for years, a stated support period with secure updates matters most, because new flaws keep appearing.
questions.pre_read: Think about what will happen to the devices' software over ten years.
questions.correct_explanation: Over ten years, new flaws will be found in the controllers' software, and only updates from the maker can fix them; signed updates also prove each update is genuine. A device with no update path stays vulnerable for its whole life. The tamper-resistant case is the runner-up: it stops hands-on attacks, but most attacks on connected devices arrive over the network.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: physical protection has value. But most attacks on connected devices come over the network, and only updates fix newly found flaws.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because one password is easy to manage. But a shared password exposes every unit once it leaks; each device needs its own.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because central control sounds easier to secure. But it is a management convenience; it does nothing to fix flaws found in the units' software.

tips: Eliminate: B shares one password across every unit, and C is a management convenience that fixes no software flaws.
Final two: D beats A because over ten years new flaws will appear and only secure updates fix them; a strong case stops only hands-on attacks.
Exam cue: for long-lived connected devices, ask how flaws will be fixed; no update path means the risk only grows.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-213 Section 3.1 (IoT Device Cybersecurity Considerations: consider the manufacturer's expectations for delivering software updates in response to discovered vulnerabilities); NIST SP 800-213 Section 2.3 (How IoT Devices May Create Security Challenges)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Buy devices with secure updates, unique passwords and a stated support period' (notes 4.1.12 Internet of Things (IoT) Security). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An optician chain has bought a small rival, whose shop network must now reach the chain's booking server. How should the network technician connect the shop's network as BEST?

options.A: Join it flat to head office to reach the booking server
options.B: Add it as its own segment reaching only the booking server
options.C: Give it its own firewalled subnet open to all head-office traffic
options.D: Join it to head office once its laptops pass an antivirus scan

questions.key_concept: A newly joined network is a separate trust zone: connect it as its own segment, with rules allowing only the traffic it needs.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the shop's network must reach, and what you know about its devices.
questions.correct_explanation: Nobody yet knows what is on the rival's network, so it joins as its own segment, with firewall rules that let booking traffic reach the one server it uses. If something there is compromised, it cannot spread freely. Joining after an antivirus scan is the runner-up: a scan helps, but one clean result does not justify broad trust or open reach.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it gives the shop the booking access it needs. But unknown devices on a flat network can also reach everything else.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a separate subnet behind a firewall sounds segmented. But a firewall that lets all head-office traffic through separates nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: scanning the laptops is a sensible check. But one clean scan does not justify open access; limit the shop to the booking traffic.

tips: Eliminate: A joins an unknown network flat to head office, and C puts up a firewall that lets all traffic through.
Final two: B beats D because a single scan cannot prove an unknown network safe; segmenting limits harm whatever is there.
Exam cue: when you cannot vouch for a network, give it its own segment and open only the paths its work requires.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 6.2.1.3 (Network Segmentation and Isolation: only explicitly authorized traffic between segments); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Systems are grouped by trust level and purpose, such as staff devices, payment systems and guests' (notes 4.2.1 Network Segmentation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A hiking gear retailer's network technician is assigning servers to firewall zones. Which server MOST clearly belongs in the screened subnet, or demilitarized zone (DMZ)?

options.A: The payroll database that only the finance staff query
options.B: The internal DNS server that staff laptops use for lookups
options.C: The public DNS server answering for the shop's own domain
options.D: The file server holding product designs for next season

questions.key_concept: The screened subnet holds servers the public must reach; servers that only staff use stay in internal zones.
questions.pre_read: Ask who must reach each server: people on the internet, or only staff?
questions.correct_explanation: Anything the public must reach belongs in the screened subnet, where the outer firewall exposes only named services and the inner firewall keeps it apart from staff systems. A public DNS server answers internet lookups for the retailer's domain, so it fits there. The internal DNS server is the runner-up: it is the same kind of server, but only staff laptops use it, so it stays inside.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because finance data needs strong protection. But that is why it stays internal; nothing on the internet should reach it directly.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it is also a DNS server. But only staff laptops use it, so it belongs in the internal zone, out of the public's reach.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because designs are shared work files. But only staff use them, and sensitive files stay deeper inside, away from public-facing servers.

tips: Eliminate: A and D hold internal data that only staff use; neither faces the public.
Final two: C beats B because the zone follows who must reach the server; the public DNS server serves the internet, the internal one serves staff.
Exam cue: the same kind of server can sit in different zones; with split DNS, the public half goes in the screened subnet and the internal half stays inside.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 3.1 (Network Layouts with Firewalls: public-facing servers on the DMZ); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7 (Boundary Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Web servers and email gateways belong there; customer databases belong in an internal zone' (notes 4.2.2 Firewall Zones and the Screened Subnet (DMZ)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A dog grooming chain's network technician is writing a training note on virtual local area networks (VLANs). Which statement about where VLANs work is MOST accurate?

options.A: Layer 1, since each VLAN is a set of physical switch ports
options.B: Layer 3, since each VLAN routes packets by IP address
options.C: Layer 3, since the VLAN tag sits inside each packet's IP header
options.D: Layer 2, since switches keep the frames of each VLAN apart

questions.key_concept: VLANs are a layer 2 switch feature; traffic between VLANs must pass a router or layer 3 switch, where it can be filtered.
questions.pre_read: Recall which device forwards frames and which device routes packets.
questions.correct_explanation: A VLAN splits one switch's ports into separate layer 2 networks, tagging frames with a VLAN number when they cross a trunk, and devices in different VLANs cannot talk directly.
