To move between VLANs, traffic must pass a router or layer 3 switch, which is where filtering belongs. Layer 1 is the runner-up: ports are physical, but VLAN membership is a switch setting, not a cable.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: VLANs are assigned to ports. But membership is a switch setting that tags frames at layer 2; layer 1 is only the physical signal.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because each VLAN acts like its own network. But routing by IP address is the layer 3 device's job between VLANs, not the VLAN's.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because VLANs are tagged. But the 802.1Q tag sits in the layer 2 frame, not in the IP header.

tips: Eliminate: B and C put VLANs at layer 3; VLANs neither route by IP address nor tag the IP header.
Final two: D beats A because VLAN membership is a layer 2 switch setting; ports are physical, but the separation is not.
Exam cue: VLAN means layer 2 separation; anything moving between VLANs meets a layer 3 device, which is where to filter.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Appendix E.1.3 (Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs): switches logically separate traffic based on switch ports); NIST SP 800-119 Section 6.4.1 (Deployment of a Dual Stack Environment: 802.1q tags can be used to divide a network logically)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'VLANs are a layer 2 switch feature; traffic between them needs a layer 3 device, where filtering happens' (notes 4.2.3 Virtual LANs (VLANs)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A mortgage broker wants micro-segmentation for 60 virtual machines on one hypervisor cluster, without buying new network hardware. Where should the system administrator propose enforcing the rules as BEST?

options.A: On the edge firewall in front of the hypervisor cluster
options.B: On the core router, filtering traffic between the data center's VLANs
options.C: On the switches, by giving each virtual machine its own physical port
options.D: In the hypervisor's virtual firewall or each machine's host firewall

questions.key_concept: Micro-segmentation is enforced close to each workload, in the hypervisor, host firewalls or cloud security groups, so it sees traffic between neighbors.
questions.pre_read: Think about which traffic each enforcement point can actually see.
questions.correct_explanation: Micro-segmentation applies policy to each workload, so enforcement must sit where every machine's traffic passes: a virtual firewall in the hypervisor or a firewall on each host. Both are software, so no new hardware is needed, and they see traffic between machines on the same host or VLAN. The core router is the runner-up: it filters between VLANs, but machines sharing a VLAN never pass it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the edge firewall is the main control. But it sees only traffic entering or leaving, not traffic between the virtual machines.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: routers do filter between VLANs. But machines on the same VLAN or host talk without passing the router at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because separate ports isolate devices. But the machines share physical hosts, and this needs the new hardware the broker wants to avoid.

tips: Eliminate: A filters only traffic crossing the internet edge, and C needs new hardware while machines still share hosts.
Final two: D beats B because enforcement in the hypervisor or host sees traffic between neighbors; the router sees only traffic between VLANs.
Exam cue: micro-segmentation lives next to the workload; if an option enforces it on a distant boundary device, look again.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-215 Section 5.1.2 (Microsegmentation – Implementation Approaches: virtual firewalls inside a hypervisor, or host-based agents using the host's native firewall); NIST SP 800-207 Section 3.1.2 (ZTA Using Micro-Segmentation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Enforcement sits close to the workload: in host firewalls, the virtualization platform or cloud security groups' (notes 4.2.4 Micro-Segmentation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Defense in depth
questions.question: A ticket resale site relies on its web application firewall (WAF) alone to stop injected commands, and testers slipped one past it. Which addition should the security analyst propose to BEST apply defense in depth?

options.A: Tighter WAF rules, so the same trick cannot get through again
options.B: Checks on every input inside the application's own code
options.C: Blocking the testers' addresses at the edge firewall
options.D: A stricter edge firewall rule set for the application's web ports

questions.key_concept: Defense in depth puts a second, independent check behind each control, so a bypass of one layer is caught by the next.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option still stops the attack after the WAF is bypassed again.
questions.correct_explanation: The WAF is one layer, and testers have shown it can be bypassed. Validating input in the application's own code adds a layer behind it: it checks each entry where it is used, whatever got past the WAF. Tighter WAF rules are the runner-up: they close this one trick, but the WAF stays the only check, so the next bypass meets nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it closes the trick the testers used. But the WAF remains the only check, so the next new bypass meets no second control.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it stops this test from repeating. But real attackers use other addresses, and the bypass itself still works.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the edge firewall guards the server. But it filters ports and addresses, and the web ports must stay open for customers.

tips: Eliminate: C blocks only the testers' addresses, which real attackers do not share, and D adds a port filter that cannot read web requests and must leave web ports open.
Final two: B beats A because tighter rules still leave the WAF as the only check; validation in the code stops what the next bypass lets through.
Exam cue: assume every layer will be bypassed one day; defense in depth asks what still stops the attack when it is.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-8(1) (Security and Privacy Architectures | Defense in Depth); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-10 (Information Input Validation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Each layer should fail independently; two controls sharing one password or one flaw are really one layer' (notes 4.2.5 Defense in Depth). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust principles
questions.question: At a fashion house adopting Zero Trust, the security analyst finds the payroll app admits any office Wi-Fi device unchecked; its system owner approves the app's access rules. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Flag the gap to the system owner, proposing a device check
options.B: Change the rule to require device checks, then tell the system owner
options.C: Leave the rule, since the office Wi-Fi is an internal network
options.D: Block every office Wi-Fi device from the app until it is fixed

questions.key_concept: Zero Trust grants nothing for network location; a rule that still trusts location goes to its owner with a proposed fix.
questions.pre_read: Check what Zero Trust says about trusting a network location, and who approves this app's rules.
questions.correct_explanation: Admitting any device because it is on the office Wi-Fi is location-based trust, which Zero Trust removes: every request should be checked for identity and device health. The system owner approves the app's access rules, so the analyst flags the gap to them with a proposed device check. Changing the rule first is the runner-up: the fix is right, but making it alone bypasses the owner's approval.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a device check is the right fix. But the system owner approves this app's access rules, so changing it first bypasses them, even if they are told afterward.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the office Wi-Fi is the company's own. But Zero Trust gives no trust for network location; every request is checked.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it closes the gap at once. But it cuts all staff off from payroll, a change the analyst has no authority to make.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts devices for being on the office network, and D shuts every staff device out, far beyond the analyst's role.
Final two: A beats B because the system owner approves the app's access rules; the analyst proposes the fix rather than making it alone.
Exam cue: Zero Trust removes trust by location; when a rule still relies on it, take it to the rule's owner with a fix.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 2.1 (Tenets of Zero Trust); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Never trust, always verify: being on the office network or a virtual private network (VPN) earns no access by itself' (notes 4.2.6 Zero Trust Principles). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust components
questions.question: A dairy cooperative is adopting Zero Trust. Which input should its policy engine use MOST directly to judge whether a staff laptop asking for access is healthy?

options.A: The laptop's IP address on the office's internal network
options.B: The user's job title in the human resources system
options.C: The device manager's record of patches and encryption
options.D: The threat feed's list of known malicious domains

questions.key_concept: A Zero Trust policy engine judges device health from inputs such as device management data on patches and encryption, not from network location.
questions.pre_read: Match each input to what it actually tells the policy engine.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy engine weighs inputs from several sources, and device health comes from the device management system, which reports each laptop's patch level, encryption and similar state. A threat feed is the runner-up: it is also a real policy input, but it describes outside threats, such as bad domains, not the condition of this laptop.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the address shows where the laptop is. But Zero Trust grants nothing for location, and an address says nothing about health.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because job title is a real access input. But it describes the user's role, not whether the laptop is patched or encrypted.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: threat feeds are real policy inputs. But they describe outside threats, such as bad domains, not this laptop's condition.

tips: Eliminate: A judges by network location, and B describes the person rather than the device.
Final two: C beats D because device health comes from device management data; a threat feed describes outside dangers, not the laptop.
Exam cue: match the policy input to the question: identity systems answer who, device management answers how healthy, threat feeds answer what is dangerous.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 3 (Logical Components of Zero Trust Architecture)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Policy inputs are sources the engine consults, such as identity systems, device management and security monitoring' (notes 4.2.7 Zero Trust Architecture Components). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Network access control
questions.question: A planetarium's IT manager says the switches' list of allowed media access control (MAC) addresses is no substitute for network access control (NAC). Which reply from the security analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Disagree; a MAC list suffices if each port admits one address
options.B: Disagree; a MAC address is fixed in hardware and cannot be faked
options.C: Agree; NAC also encrypts traffic between each device and the switch
options.D: Agree; NAC also verifies each device's credentials and health

questions.key_concept: A MAC list checks only an address the device announces; NAC authenticates devices with credentials or certificates and checks their health.
questions.pre_read: Compare what each control actually verifies about a device.
questions.correct_explanation: The IT manager is right. A MAC list checks only an address the device announces, and software can copy an allowed one. NAC authenticates each device with credentials or certificates, often through 802.1X, and checks its health, such as patches and antivirus, before granting access. One address per port is the runner-up: it limits how many devices join, but a copied address still gets in.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: one address per port does stop extra devices joining. But a device that copies the allowed address still gets in, unchecked.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because makers assign MAC addresses. But software can change the address a device presents, so allowed ones are easily copied.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because NAC guards the network edge. But NAC decides which devices join and how far; it does not encrypt their traffic.

tips: Eliminate: B treats MAC addresses as fixed, though software can change them, and C credits NAC with encryption, which is not its job.
Final two: D beats A because NAC checks credentials and health; limiting each port to one address still admits a copied address.
Exam cue: when asked whether one control can replace another, list what each actually verifies; a stand-in that checks less is not a substitute.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.7 (Network Access Control: health checks and limited access for remediation); NIST SP 800-94 Section 5.1.2 (WLAN Components: SSIDs are broadcast in plaintext, so any listening device can learn them, and MAC addresses are relatively trivial to spoof)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Media access control (MAC) address filtering protects as well as NAC is a trap: MAC addresses are easy to copy, while NAC authenticates and checks health' (notes 4.2.8 Network Access Control (NAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. AI development environments
questions.question: A recipe app company's artificial intelligence (AI) experiment servers can reach every internal database, because all of them sit inside the network. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep full reach, since the experiments run on internal servers
options.B: Copy every production database onto the experiment segment
options.C: Allow flows only to the approved, masked datasets they use
options.D: Require multifactor sign-in for staff on the experiment servers

questions.key_concept: AI experiment segments get only the data flows they need, using approved, masked data; being internal earns no open reach.
questions.pre_read: Consider what an experiment server could reach if it were misused or compromised.
questions.correct_explanation: Internal does not mean trusted: experiment servers are often less hardened than production, so open reach to every database makes them an easy path for leaks and poisoning. Allowing only flows to the approved, masked datasets keeps experiments working while cutting that path. Multifactor sign-in is the runner-up: it protects who logs in, but the servers themselves could still reach every database.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because everything stays inside the network. But internal does not mean trusted; a misused experiment server could read or alter any database.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes the network flows. But it puts real production data on less protected servers, the risk masked data avoids.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: MFA strengthens sign-in. But it limits who logs in, not where the servers can reach; one compromise still reaches every database.

tips: Eliminate: A treats internal as trusted, and B copies real production data onto less protected experiment servers.
Final two: C beats D because the problem is the servers' reach; MFA guards sign-ins but leaves every database open to them.
Exam cue: for AI development, limit both the data and the paths to it; an internal location grants nothing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-3(2) (System Development Life Cycle | Use of Live or Operational Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI development servers are internal, so they may reach production data and the internet, is a trap: internal does not mean trusted' (notes 4.2.9 Segmenting AI Development Environments). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A national lottery's results website automatically adds servers when draw results go live, then removes them an hour later. Which essential cloud characteristic does the system administrator see MOST directly?

options.A: Rapid elasticity
options.B: Resource pooling
options.C: Measured service
options.D: On-demand self-service

questions.key_concept: Rapid elasticity is capacity growing and shrinking quickly with demand; resource pooling is the provider sharing hardware among customers.
questions.pre_read: Focus on what changes in this scenario, and when it changes.
questions.correct_explanation: Rapid elasticity means capacity scales out and back in quickly, often automatically, to match demand, as the lottery's servers do when results go live. Resource pooling is the runner-up: the provider does serve many customers from shared hardware, which makes elasticity possible, but pooling describes that sharing, not one customer's capacity growing and shrinking.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: pooling is what lets capacity appear so fast. But it describes the provider sharing hardware among customers, not one customer scaling.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the extra servers will show up on the bill. But measured service is about metering use, not capacity changing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the servers appear without a ticket. But self-service means customers set things up themselves; growing and shrinking with demand is elasticity.

tips: Eliminate: C is about metering and billing, and D is about customers setting up resources themselves, not scaling with demand.
Final two: A beats B because the clue is capacity growing and shrinking with demand; pooling is the shared hardware behind it.
Exam cue: 'scales up and down with demand' signals rapid elasticity; 'shared hardware among customers' signals resource pooling.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: essential characteristics)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Rapid elasticity and resource pooling mean the same thing is a trap: pooling is shared hardware, elasticity is capacity growing and shrinking with demand' (notes 4.3.1 The Five Essential Characteristics of Cloud Computing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A dating app company's developer runs every container in privileged mode, with full access to the host, to avoid permission errors. Which change should the system administrator propose as BEST?

options.A: Scan every image for known flaws, and keep privileged mode
options.B: Keep privileged mode, since containers are as isolated as VMs
options.C: Drop privileged mode only for the containers facing the internet
options.D: Run them unprivileged, with only the rights each one needs

questions.key_concept: A privileged container can act as part of the host and affect every other container on it; run containers with only the rights they need.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a compromised container could reach in each setup.
questions.correct_explanation: Containers share the host's kernel, and privileged mode removes most of the walls between a container and the host. If any one container is compromised, the attacker can act as the host and reach every other container on it. Running unprivileged, with only needed rights, limits that. Scanning images is the runner-up: it finds known flaws, but unknown flaws and stolen credentials still get in.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: scanning images finds known flaws. But unknown flaws and stolen credentials still get in, and privileged mode then hands over the host.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because containers feel separate. But they share the host's kernel, and privileged mode removes most of the walls left between them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because internet-facing containers are the likeliest targets. But any compromised container in privileged mode can still take over the host.

tips: Eliminate: B treats containers as isolated as virtual machines, and C leaves privileged mode on containers that can still be compromised.
Final two: D beats A because scanning catches only known flaws; removing privilege limits the damage from any compromise.
Exam cue: when a setting removes isolation, reduce privilege first; detection tools help, but least privilege limits the blast.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-190 Section 3.4.3 (Insecure container runtime configurations: a container run in privileged mode can act as part of the host OS and impact all other containers); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Containers are as isolated from each other as virtual machines is a trap: containers share the host's kernel, so one kernel flaw can affect them all' (notes 4.3.2 Virtualization and Containers in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A pottery supplier's security team wants to keep its monitoring agent on the booking servers after bookings move to a software as a service (SaaS) product. Which reply from the system administrator is MOST accurate?

options.A: SaaS gives no server access, so watch the service's audit logs
options.B: Ask the service provider to install the firm's agent on its servers
options.C: Install the agent through the SaaS admin console after the move
options.D: Monitoring now falls to the provider, so the agent is not needed

questions.key_concept: In SaaS the customer manages no servers, so it watches its own use through the service's audit logs rather than server agents.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a SaaS customer controls, and what it can still see.
questions.correct_explanation: In SaaS the provider runs the servers, operating systems and application, so the customer cannot place its own agents there. Monitoring does not end, though: the customer still watches its own users and data, through the service's audit logs and admin reports. Asking the provider to install the agent is the runner-up: it keeps the familiar tool, but providers run shared infrastructure and do not host customers' agents.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it tries to keep the familiar tool. But the provider runs shared servers for many customers and does not install customers' agents.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the console controls the service. But SaaS consoles manage users and settings, not software on the provider's servers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider now runs the servers. But the firm still watches its own users and data, using the service's logs.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes SaaS customers can install software on provider servers, and D hands the firm's own monitoring to the provider.
Final two: A beats B because SaaS gives the customer no server access at all; its view comes from the service's own audit logs.
Exam cue: as the service model moves up, your tools move up too: from server agents to the logs and settings the service exposes.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'SaaS delivers a finished application; the customer manages users, settings and the data it puts in' (notes 4.3.3 Cloud Service Models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bakers' trade association runs cloud services built for its members' food-safety records, and only member bakeries may sign up. Which deployment model should the association's security analyst record as MOST accurate?

options.A: A private cloud
options.B: A community cloud
options.C: A hybrid cloud
options.D: A public cloud

questions.key_concept: A community cloud serves several organizations with common needs and excludes others; a private cloud serves one organization.
questions.pre_read: Count how many organizations use the services, and what they have in common.
questions.correct_explanation: A community cloud serves a group of separate organizations with shared concerns, here the same food-safety record needs, and excludes everyone outside the group; members must agree who manages access and security. A private cloud is the runner-up: it also excludes outsiders, but it serves just one organization, while many separate bakeries use these services.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it also excludes outsiders. But a private cloud serves one organization, and many separate bakeries use these services.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because several parties are involved. But hybrid means joining different deployment models, and this is one set of services.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because many businesses use it. But a public cloud is open to any customer, and only member bakeries may sign up here.

tips: Eliminate: C needs a mix of deployment models, and D is open to any customer.
Final two: B beats A because private means one organization; several organizations with shared needs make a community cloud.
Exam cue: identify the model by who uses it: anyone (public), one organization (private), a group with shared needs (community), a mix (hybrid).
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: deployment models)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A community cloud is shared by organizations with common needs' (notes 4.3.4 Cloud Deployment Models). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A county parks department uses infrastructure, platform and software as a service (IaaS, PaaS and SaaS). Which security duty should its security analyst list as MOST clearly the department's in all three?

options.A: Patching the operating system under each service
options.B: Fixing flaws in the department's own application code
options.C: Securing the data center buildings that host the services
options.D: Deciding who can access the department's data and accounts

questions.key_concept: Data, accounts and access stay with the customer in every cloud model; other layers move to the provider as models go from IaaS to SaaS.
questions.pre_read: Walk each duty through IaaS, PaaS and SaaS and see where it changes hands.
questions.correct_explanation: In every model the customer decides who can reach its data, manages its accounts and sets its own access rules; that never moves to the provider. Other duties shift as the model changes. Fixing application code is the runner-up: the department owns its code in IaaS and PaaS, but in SaaS the provider writes and fixes the application.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the department patches its own servers in IaaS. But in PaaS and SaaS the provider patches the operating system.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the department owns its code in IaaS and PaaS. But in SaaS the provider writes and fixes the application.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because buildings need protecting. But data center security is the provider's in every model, never the customer's.

tips: Eliminate: A applies only to IaaS, and C is always the provider's job.
Final two: D beats B because data and access stay with the customer in every model; application code moves to the provider in SaaS.
Exam cue: for 'in every model' questions, test each option against SaaS, where the customer holds least; a duty that survives there is the customer's everywhere.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The customer always owns its data, accounts, access rights and service configuration' (notes 4.3.5 The Shared Responsibility Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A tutoring platform put all its infrastructure as a service (IaaS) virtual machines in one zone, and a zone outage took it offline. Under shared responsibility, who MOST clearly should have spread them across zones?

options.A: The provider, since its agreement with the platform covers uptime
options.B: The tutoring platform, since it chooses where its machines run
options.C: The provider, since it should move machines between zones itself
options.D: Nobody, since cloud services stay available by design

questions.key_concept: In IaaS the provider offers separate zones, but designing the customer's own workloads to survive a zone outage is the customer's job.
questions.pre_read: Ask who decides where the virtual machines run in IaaS.
questions.correct_explanation: In IaaS the provider runs the zones and keeps each one as reliable as its agreement says, but the customer decides where its own machines run. Placing every machine in one zone was the platform's choice, so spreading them across zones was its job. The service level agreement is the runner-up: it sets an uptime target and a remedy, such as credits, not the customer's design.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the agreement does set an uptime target. But it promises a target and credits, not the design of the customer's own machines.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the provider runs the zones. But in IaaS the customer places and manages its own machines; the provider does not redesign them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because cloud services are built for resilience. But a workload placed in a single zone fails along with that zone.

tips: Eliminate: C expects the provider to rearrange the customer's machines, and D assumes the cloud is resilient whatever the design.
Final two: B beats A because the agreement sets a target and a remedy, not the platform's design; placing machines is the customer's choice.
Exam cue: the provider offers resilient building blocks; using them to keep your own workload running is your job.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models); NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.8 (Availability: 99.95% availability still means about 4.38 hours of downtime a year)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The provider owns security of the cloud; the customer owns security in the cloud' (notes 4.3.5 The Shared Responsibility Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.3 Cloud security. Cloud roles and agreements
questions.question: A fishing cooperative's IT coordinator notes its cloud traffic travels to the provider over a telecom firm's leased line. Which National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) cloud actor is the telecom firm MOST accurately?

options.A: A cloud broker
options.B: A cloud carrier
options.C: A cloud auditor
options.D: A cloud provider

questions.key_concept: In NIST's reference architecture, a cloud carrier provides the connectivity and transport between cloud consumers and providers.
questions.pre_read: Match the telecom firm's job to each actor's role.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST names five cloud actors. The carrier provides connectivity and transport of cloud services between consumers and providers, which is exactly what the telecom firm's leased line does. The broker is the runner-up: it is also a go-between, but it manages, combines or negotiates cloud services for the consumer rather than carrying the traffic.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a broker is also a go-between. But it manages or combines services and negotiates with providers; it does not carry traffic.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an outside firm is involved. But a cloud auditor independently assesses cloud services; it carries no traffic.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the firm supplies a service. But the provider runs the cloud service itself; the telecom only carries traffic to it.

tips: Eliminate: C assesses cloud services independently, and D runs the cloud service; neither carries the traffic.
Final two: B beats A because the telecom firm transports traffic; a broker manages or combines services for the consumer.
Exam cue: carrier carries, broker brokers, auditor assesses; match the actor to the verb in the scenario.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 500-292 Section 2.6 (Cloud Carrier: an intermediary that provides connectivity and transport of cloud services between cloud consumers and cloud providers)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Cloud carrier: the network or telecom provider that carries traffic between consumers and providers' (notes 4.3.6 Cloud Roles and Agreements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A weather analytics startup encrypts its artificial intelligence (AI) training data in cloud storage with keys kept only on one administrator's laptop, outside the provider. Which risk should the security analyst rate GREATEST?

options.A: Losing that laptop would leave the training data unreadable for good
options.B: The provider could decrypt the training data whenever it chose
options.C: The training data sits unencrypted, since the keys are kept elsewhere
options.D: The laptop's uploads to the cloud would no longer use TLS

questions.key_concept: Customer-held keys shield data from the provider, but if the only copy of the keys is lost, the data is gone for good.
questions.pre_read: Consider who holds the keys, and what happens if that holder fails.
questions.correct_explanation: Holding the keys outside the provider is what stops the provider from reading the data, so that risk is low here. The new risk is that one laptop holds the only copy: if it is lost, stolen or fails, nothing can decrypt the training data again. Provider access is the runner-up: it is the main risk when the provider manages the keys, but customer-held keys remove it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: provider access is the usual worry. But it applies when the provider manages the keys; keys held only by the startup block it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the keys are not with the data. But keeping keys apart is how encryption works; the stored data stays encrypted.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the keys sit on that laptop. But TLS protects data in transit no matter where the storage keys are kept.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses keeping keys elsewhere with leaving data unencrypted, and D mixes up storage keys with TLS for data in transit.
Final two: A beats B because customer-held keys stop provider access; with a single copy on one laptop, losing it loses the data.
Exam cue: whoever holds the keys holds the data; check both who else can use them and what happens if the only copy is lost.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-12(1) (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management | Availability); NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.7 (Data Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Keys can be provider-managed, customer-managed inside the provider's key service, or held only by the customer' (notes 4.3.7 Protecting Data in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: By procedure, a printing firm's security analyst deletes access keys idle over 60 days in any company cloud account; a scan finds one idle 200 days. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Rotate the key, so any copy of the old one stops working
options.B: Leave the key, since the provider retires unused keys itself
options.C: Cut the key to read-only rights, and record it on the scan
options.D: Delete the key, and record the change on the scan finding

questions.key_concept: An unused cloud key should be removed, not rotated or weakened; when the procedure assigns removal, the analyst does it and records it.
questions.pre_read: Check what the procedure already assigns, and to whom.
questions.correct_explanation: Stale access keys are a common cloud misconfiguration: anyone who finds an old key gets its rights, and nobody is watching it. The procedure gives the analyst the job of deleting keys idle over 60 days, so deleting this one and recording the change is the in-role step. Rotating it is the runner-up: it stops leaked copies of the old secret, but leaves a working key that nothing needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: rotating does stop leaked copies of the old key. But it leaves a fresh, working credential that nothing needs, and the procedure says delete.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because providers offer key tools. But keys and permissions are customer settings, and an unused key stays valid until the customer removes it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it reduces the key's power and records the change. But a forgotten key that can still read data keeps the exposure open.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves a customer setting to the provider, and C keeps a forgotten credential active with access to data.
Final two: D beats A because rotation still leaves a working key that does no work; deleting it closes the door, as the procedure directs.
Exam cue: an unused credential does no work but still opens doors; remove it rather than refresh or weaken it.

questions.question: A tax firm's client contracts require data to stay in its home country, and its cloud artificial intelligence (AI) service's processing region is still set to 'any'. Which step should the system administrator take FIRST?

options.A: Ask the provider to keep the firm's prompts in its home country
options.B: Encrypt prompts sent to the service, which keeps them within the rules
options.C: Leave the processing region as is, since the provider decides it
options.D: Set the AI service's processing region to the firm's home country

questions.key_concept: Where a cloud AI service processes data is often a customer setting, and meeting data-location duties stays the customer's job.
questions.pre_read: Check who controls the service's settings, including where it runs.
questions.correct_explanation: The service lets customers choose where prompts are processed, so meeting the contracts' location rule is a setting the firm controls: it sets the region to the home country before client data is sent. Asking the provider is the runner-up: the provider does run the regions, but this choice is already the customer's, and the firm stays accountable for its client data.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the provider runs the regions. But the service already gives the firm this setting, and the firm stays accountable for meeting its contracts.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption protects prompts. But it protects them on the way; they would still be processed in another country.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the provider runs the service. But where the firm's data goes is a customer setting, and the contracts bind the firm.

tips: Eliminate: B mistakes encryption in transit for keeping data in the country, and C hands a customer setting to the provider.
Final two: D beats A because the region is already a customer setting; the firm meets its own contracts by setting it.
Exam cue: an AI service is still a cloud service; if a setting decides where your data goes, setting it is your job.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.2 (Compliance: data location is one of the most common compliance issues, and organizations remain accountable for data a provider holds for them); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed)
